The climate crisis demands a significant shift in mindset and behavior from each of us to ensure our collective survival. Traditional public climate change communication often highlights scientific proof and the necessity of action, but a new, more relatable approach is now being explored - leveraging the concept of personal values to inspire behavioral change. Cloudflare has initiated a project, called the Values Action Insights Laboratory (VALS), to investigate how individual climate actions can be aligned with their underlying personal values. By integrating climate action tracking with natural language processing and other value-based metrics, VALS provides a unique platform that helps individuals uncover the climate actions most meaningful to them. Using an adaptable, customizable data analysis structure allows the lab to analyze diverse sets of data and offer personalized insights into individual preferences for actions like transportation, consumption, and more. As VALS evolves with more diverse user input, the lab will gain a deeper understanding of individual connections between values and actions, ultimately guiding more effective value-aligned climate actions.

In healthcare NLP, extracting clinical symptoms from patient descriptions despite their complexity and ambiguity, has been a challenging problem.  Despite the growing availability of large electronic health records, learning symptom representation remains difficult due to data privacy restrictions and limited labeled data.  To address this issue, we aim to enhance symptom extractor performance across various clinical datasets, which may stem from different sources and therefore involve distinct semantic and linguistic characteristics.  Leveraging the emerging technique of domain generalization, we successfully trained a model to accurately interpret symptoms across multiple clinical domains using the electronic health data.  In doing so, we achieved state-of-the-art performance in several datasets, which outperformed existing methods by a significant margin.  As such, our findings provide valuable insights for the healthcare NLP community in extracting meaningful symptoms from diverse clinical settings.

Our approach leverages the observation that recurrent neural networks in deep neural networks can be reinterpreted as iterative optimization methods. We use this interpretation to design an alternative training algorithm for RNNs within end-to-end autonomous driving systems, which our results show leads to superior performance even in scenarios with limited visibility. This improved efficiency also enables the efficient training of larger models with more parameters. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experimental evaluations of autonomous driving tasks under both visible and non-visible conditions. Notably, our results demonstrate that vehicle trajectory prediction tasks with limited visibility become significantly more accurate with the inclusion of an RNN component, yielding a 20% relative gain in mAP metrics, even in extreme cases where the visible period is as short as one second. In contrast, comparable improvements in performance without the inclusion of RNNs can only be achieved by increasing vehicle trajectory dataset size in a highly substantial manner - a 4.5-fold increase - which may not be a feasible option in many real-world applications due to the immense time and resources required to collect such a large dataset.

We propose that RNNs can be universally applied as effective classifiers. Specifically, our research introduces the RNN-based classifier that rivals the performance of traditional ANNs while consuming significantly less power. The classifier is defined as an RNN with a matrix dimension that matches the number of data features, thus eliminating the need for specific RNN temporal properties to be exploited. We observe that such RNNs converge to similarity matrices that are nearly complete, thereby functionally approximating similarity-based kernel methods. This insight is further reinforced by a theoretical analogy that compares RNNs to kernel support vector machines. Through numerical experiments, our research also highlights the potential for RNNs to be trained in supervised and unsupervised settings to classify data, a discovery that is further validated through analysis. Ultimately, our research concludes that RNNs can be an effective and versatile classifier, as illustrated by open-source implementations available at https://github.com/ryzhykov/RNN-Universal-Classifier.

We present the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field. To account for the effect of the magnetic field on the matter's properties, we modified the equation of state for non-relativistic matter by incorporating a magnetic field correction. We further derived an expression for strange quark $K^-$ hypernuclei and applied it to compact stars. To represent spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field, we developed a matter model. This includes a magnetic energy density term and we computed the matter's total energy density, pressure, and speed of sound. We demonstrated how the matter's compressibility, pressure, and other properties are influenced by spin polarization and a strong magnetic field. The impact of these factors on neutron stars, particularly their radius, mass, and buoyancy, is examined, and we examined the buoyancy of strange stars in a strong magnetic field.

The Personal Data Alliance's (PDA) Pando platform enables individuals to pool their underutilized device processing capabilities, creating a distributed cloud environment where computation and data remain under user control and privacy is safeguarded. By leveraging mobile app and API connections, as well as an optimized routing algorithm, PDA maximizes the available processing power and accelerates computation speeds. In a performance evaluation, PDA outperformed single-device computation by a factor of 1.5 to 2, while outperforming equivalent server-based cloud solutions (Dropbox and Amazon S3) in cryptography and digital signing operations, and excelling in image processing, as well as code and document data transfers.

We present an innovative numerical method for determining eigenvalues and eigenvectors of compact self-adjoint operators. By incorporating adaptive sampling techniques, our approach enhances the efficiency of n-dimensional numerical n-eigensystem approximation. The results from each iteration of the method serve as a guide for sampling the next stage, often allowing for a decrease in the dimensionality of the problem. The combination of this adaptivity with Landau's optimal quadrature rule leads to highly accurate computations. The efficiency and precision of our method are demonstrated through numerical tests in this paper.

We provide a detailed characterization, in terms of verification conditions, 
of the topological and Baire category properties of the survivor sets of all 
non-integer intermediate beta-transformations. 
Essentially, each set is closed and corresponds to the set of best 
approximable numbers of a specific type of diophantine nature. 
It also happens to be homeomorphic to the space of badly approximable numbers 
of a specific non-integer base. 
Furthermore, we demonstrate that these sets are countably many and dense 
in their respective semi-orbits. 
This result allows us to identify sets with positive Hausdorff dimension, 
including a $C$-large collection, where $C$ denotes a constant strictly less 
than one, of the intermediate beta-transformations with survivor sets having 
a positive Lebesgue measure.

We examine SO(Nc) gauge theories with Nf quark flavors using lattice simulations, focusing on which symmetries remain after quantum effects and how the gluon field influences these symmetries. Theories with Nf=5 to 8 display a SU(Nf) x SU(Nf) chiral symmetry with five or seven Goldstone bosons, respectively, consistent with lattice expectations in the deep interior. The long-range behavior shows a broken U(1)B symmetry, which we interpret as an axial U(1) anomaly. In the deep interior, the gluon field breaks a U(1)AX symmetry involving the axial phase of the quark. We interpret this as a deconfinement phase, with the gluon field spontaneously breaking a discrete chiral symmetry at a finite temperature or chemical potential.

We propose a new method, Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC), which enables the precise tracking of time-varying importance within complex data sets. We applied DAC to analyze the effects of weather on discrete, time-dependent variables - specifically, whether a user chooses to ride one, two, or three bikes - while accounting for the impact of weather conditions such as temperature, wind speed, and rain. Our DAC approach successfully isolated the individual impacts of each weather factor across distinct time scales, discovering that wind speed has a disentangled influence on each discrete outcome, whereas other factors like temperature and rain have overlapping impacts on these outcomes. We validated our method using a real-world bike-sharing data set, achieving striking visual results, and demonstrated the scalability of DAC to analyze high-dimensional time-series data, such as, a million days of weather data, within a short period of time.

In federated learning, various approaches have been proposed to protect user data, however most only offer partial privacy guarantees due to flaws in methods. Current solutions also incur unnecessary communication costs and excessive computational requirements. To address these issues, we introduce FedDPV, an end-to-far end learning system that ensures total privacy between clients and the central server. By utilizing internal verification, FedDPV detects and discards inaccurate gradient data, thereby allowing the server to make do without performing its own expensive differential privacy operations. Our experiments show that FedDPV produces models with comparable accuracy while reducing both the fourfold communication cost and the massive computational burden associated with prior work.

We developed a fully open-source solution for on-the-spot driver testing on a wide range of microcontrollers based on RISC architecture. Our software consists of three main components: DTestDriver creates a cyclic pattern test function that uses a driver's specific testing methods; DTestHarness uses a configuration system to orchestrate drivers and a builder that adapts different interfaces; finally, the MicroBuilder customises a firmware built from the two previous modules based on a selected controller's architecture.

This study introduces Timeloops, a cutting-edge solution for security research that enables deep and wide system call filtering for programs run in interpreted languages such as PHP and Python. Building on previous work that used virtual machines to replicate application behavior, Timeloops interprets code on a single-threaded system-on-chip that is both particularly efficient and offers a highly detailed binary interface. Furthermore, by enabling the creation of varied execution environments with different file systems, Timeloops enables that both an application's functional needs and its malicious behavior can be carefully guided on real devices, even when this application has numerous entry points and unanticipated actions. As a result, successful use of real-world affected systems like the CNAP campaign and Python-enabled log4j vulnerability indicates that Timeloops facilitates deep and broad system call filtering and makes this solution accessible and efficient.

Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) datasets contain substantial sparsity due to technical sequencing issues, which hindering effective data analysis. Traditional dimensionality reduction techniques fail to optimize low-dimensional representations due to their reliance on traditional distance metrics, which do not account for the sparsity. This issue has led researchers to apply zero-avoiding distributions, but this approach has limited the design of specialized algorithms. Our work focuses on high-performance dimensionality reduction methods for scRNA-seq data by introducing a framework based on low-dimensional product spaces with optimized metrics. We assess the efficiency of our methods by conducting a large-scale experiment on 1,156 datasets, which revealed improved performance in classification and clustering tasks in low-dimensional product spaces over Euclidean metrics, with gains of up to 40% and 20%, respectively. Additionally, our methods have led to the development of two novel variants, which achieved state-of-the-art results in real-data clustering accuracy and processing speed, respectively.

For a supermassive black hole that is surrounded by a cluster of lesser-mass stars, we are studying the superrelaxation process in which low-energy, unbound stellar objects collide and scatter high-energy, runaway stars. We are modeling the differential scattering rate of these low-mass stars by integrating over a power-law distribution of masses, which also accounts for the influence of the supermassive black hole's gravitational pull. We are using past research on unbound orbital dynamics and recent findings on radial velocity dispersion to estimate the distribution of low-mass stars, which reveals the significance of objects with a mass around the brown dwarf range. We are demonstrating how weak self-gravity among low-mass stars in a supermassive black hole's surroundings can lead to a considerable number of super-scatterings near the event horizon. We are noting the sensitivity of the scattering rate to the presence of a central bar and a disk in the galactic core. We are highlighting the potential for low-mass stars in a supermassive black hole's surroundings to produce a considerable number of super-scatterings without requiring an exceptionally low stellar mass distribution.

This research aims to provide an overview of existing strategies for integrating stochastic models and predictive control within a unified framework. Following an introduction of key concepts in Section 2, the primary methods for handling uncertainty in Section 3, while supplementary information on probabilistic distribution and optimization is provided in Section 4, 5, and 6, respectively. Ultimately, existing approaches and open challenges are discussed in Section 7.

Independent Component Analysis (ICA) and its abbreviated version (PCA) are广泛用于处理数据压缩和非线性问题. 这篇论文提出了一种适用于压縮混合矩阵的增强算法. 实验结果显示,该算法能够与伊恩-沃克提出的传统 ICA 方法相抗衡,同时其计算效果与高维数据下 ICA 的方法相当.进一步地,该论文还比较了两种解决压縮 ICA 问题的算法.实验证实,虽然基于梯度下降的算法可以解决压縮 ICA 问题,但其性能远不如拟态熵算法.在内存使用方面,该论文提出的算法与传统 ICA 方法相比,分别节约了 50%和 66%的内存.相比传统压缩 ICA 算法,该论文提出的算法在性能上分别提升了 1.3 和 2.5 倍,同时其在高维数据环境下的计算效果得以保留.

We investigate the dynamics of an open voter model that results from augmenting a symmetric two-species interaction with noise on a complete graph. This graph consists of numerous nodes, each connected to an external source of randomly flipped species. This construction serves as an effective means to model the noise in an asymmetric voter model that acts upon a linear lattice of points. This novel model that incorporates noise has two variants, an asymmetric version and a symmetric version. Through the analysis of the model, we find that, regardless of the type (asymmetric or symmetric), the competition between two species can result in either one species dominating or both co-existing. This asymmetry vs. symmetry distinction affects the parameters at which the phase transition between these two outcomes occurs. Additionally, the model exhibits critical behavior, both in time and space. This behavior is exposable by applying the techniques of renormalization to both the time and space variables.

This research explores the entanglement between two oscillators driven by thermal noise and a feedback control system in a continuous loop. The two oscillators' damped motion is mode-converted to create entangled output streams. The study employs a model using quantum stochastic differential equations to create exact expressions for the entanglement's behavior, which are then verified numerically. The results show that the feedback control system significantly enhances the system's ability to resist thermal effects, leading to greater entanglement between the oscillators. Notably, the feedback control's presence also improves entanglement against technical noise. Moreover, the study demonstrates a crucial balance in feedback control strength to avoid amplifying quantum noise and losing entanglement. The results are supported by specific examples, including the parametric cooling of an oscillator and the dual-drive optomechanical entanglement, and are anticipated to provide valuable guidance for improving entanglement in feedback-controlled quantum systems.

A general method is introduced for creating subtraction terms in N$^{k-1}$LL PHETQCD line singularities at multiple poles, with its initial application being at the one-loop level for triple-collinear configurations. This leads to the development of a novel triple-collinear splitting operator. This operator is essential in phetQCD for correctly handling re-emit and re-reordering effects in triple-collinear and nested triple-collinear phase spaces, with forms that align closely with traditional splitting functions. We have integrated this operator into aphid, PhetQCD's subtraction library, adding support for N$^1$LL PHETQCD triple-collinear and nested triple-collinear splitting functions. This is the first time such operators have been defined for this order. This splitting library has been used to verify re-order and re-order nested triple-collinear contributions at one-loop order in PhetQCD. We have also defined corresponding splitting operators for N$^1$LL PHETQCD T-odd configurations and incorporated them into the splitting library. This is the first time such operators have been defined for this order. The library has been used to verify nested T-odd and re-order T-odd splitting functions at one-loop order in PhetQCD. This work has enabled the computation of T-odd and re-order nested splitting functions at one-loop order for N$^1$LL PHETQCD. This work has

We adapt and extend two significant theories from algebraic number theory within the framework of commutative algebra. Firstly, we expand upon Greenberg's strong approximation theorem for one-dimensional local rings. Secondly, we develop an analog of Krasner's approximation lemma specifically tailored for complete local rings.

This study proposes an innovative approach to conducting sundial research in Indonesia through citizen science, a strategy that has yet to be extensively explored in Indonesian context. The primary goal is to enhance documentation, study, and the development of sundials by engaging the public. A comprehensive approach is adopted, blending philosophy, history, and especially geography as the core framework. Building on existing theory and methodologies related to sundials, citizen science, and their application in geography education, this research executes its findings by collaborating with non-geography experts to develop and publish an app for determining local noon and publishing data using the Structured Observation, Documentation, and Dissemination of Sundials method. The results show successful public engagement, resulting in over 20,000 app downloads and data collection from sundials in 27 out of 34 Indonesian regions.

This paper's proposed scheme, called the Disseminated Energy-Information Enabled Data 2D Communication System (DED2D), builds upon the observed energy and data exchanges in a line-of-sight environment. The transducer's time-division framework (TDTI) utilizes the incoming data and energy transfers to boost the transmission power of the involved nodes. By comparing the optimal solutions of the TDTI-based system and optimal data transfer only systems, we derived the TFIY (Fully Initialized Yield) scheme. However, to maximize data transfers, we initially need to allocate energy to the involved nodes, which we addressed by introducing the Optimal Energy Allocation (OEA) approach. Furthermore, we applied the OEA to transform the initial energy stored in the nodes of TFIY into its optimal configuration, which we termed Re-initialization. By incorporating an initial energy exchange as part of the system, we achieved optimal energy allocations and increased the efficiency of the involved nodes. Finally, we conducted several simulations using a Python environment to verify the proposed system's effectiveness and increased data transfer capabilities, which were not possible with the prior data transfer only system. Notably, these simulations also revealed that the involved nodes' storage capacity has minimal impact on the outcomes, validating the need for initial energy allocation.

The rise in distant control and automated experimentation demands has been particularly highlighted by the increased need for remote work requirements. To address this, a new control system called ATOM has been created to facilitate the setup of complex experiments from a distance. ATOM combines image processing and digital logic to simulate the precise movement of an experimental setup, ensuring accurate replication of experiments and streamlining the setup process. To manage this, ATOM employs a user-friendly interface based on a system programming language called Pico, which operates in conjunction with a robotic arm called an OptoTaco.

We are looking at the class of spectra for regular undirected graphs that are both partite and bounded in degree, along with their directed and non-regular counterparts. Our main result shows that when we limit the class of spectra to undirected graphs with bipartite properties, we end up with Asser's conjecture for the entire class of spectra (P = NP). Additionally, we prove that when we consider the full class of directed spectra (spectra of directed graphs), we get the P = NP result under a stronger condition. Lastly, we show that when we consider the full class of non-regular spectra (spectra of graphs, not necessarily bipartite), we end up P = NP under a stronger condition. These results are derived by reducing the respective problems to our target problems and also illustrate the limitations of a similar reduction strategy for the original P = NP problem.

A new method of calculating electrostatic phase plate profiles for phase contrast transmission electron microscopy has been developed. By modeling the phase plate with a customizable design, researchers can optimize its geometric parameters to minimize electron probe size and control current density. Furthermore, this approach is compatible with various patterns of phase plate pixels.

In 1996, Chittin and Ruvolo first proposed a universal framework for physical computation. This framework defines a computation as a fundamental property inherent to any universal calculation, applicable to classical mechanisms like Turing machines, tunneling processes, and quantum computing. Each mechanism's compliance with the framework is universally valid, calculated independently of specific implementations. However, the framework currently can't be used to distinguish novel quantum algorithms because it's been difficult to demonstrate new properties for computation. This limitation stems from the computational equivalence theorem by Nielsen and Meudinger, which suggested that quantum computing's compliance with the framework was due to existing properties. This paper aims to show that the framework's evaluation method is essentially a form of simulation. This finding opens up the possibility of using simulation-based differences between classical and quantum computing to develop an effective tool for identifying and developing new quantum algorithms.

This report addresses a counting problem related to the number of distinct locations visited by a $N$-step random walk in the counts, half counts and $1/n$ counts. These classifications were initially explored by Szekeres and in 2019 were extended by Baryshnikov and Sverak who studied a different type of counting. The report presents the derivation of the large $N$ asymptotics of these quantities for both the cases explored by these researchers. The analysis is more intricate for lower dimensional cases and a new approach is needed to understand these quantities. This is achieved by using an alternative representation for the count based on the relative positions of the walk values, known as the count process. The relative positions can be modeled as a random permutation weighted according to the spatial arrangement given by the count, semi-count and $1/n$ counts. The count, weights and relative positions can be analyzed using the properties of the random walk and the central limit theorem. By utilizing these quantities the large $N$ asymptotics can be determined. The report is more of a supplementary analysis and does not contain a numerical implementation code but presents an alternative approach which can be used to verify the previously derived results.

In this research, we explore a polymer black hole, an exact solution to the Einstein equations, which we interpret as a wormhole and analyze its properties in great detail. This solution, discovered by Oliva and Salgado, is based on a relativistic fluid with anomalous characteristics, modeled after quantum geometry in loop quantum gravity. We investigate the curvature of the spacetime, which reveals a wormhole structure devoid of horizons. Through graphical representation, we demonstrate the similarity of the curvature to a Schwarzschild black hole at a distance, while also computing the Riemann, Ricci, and Kullback-Leibler distances. We find that the curvature converges to that of Schwarzschild black holes as the curvature length scale increases. We calculate the volume of spacetime, finding that the resulting space is finite, but also that the spacetime is incomplete, signaling a potential singularity and the need for the integration of this spacetime with another, possibly describing the Big Bang. We calculate the tidal force tensor, which does not present infinite values, but does signal the presence of a timelike curvature singularity at the origin. We calculate the tidal forces, which, while not preventing an object from crossing the critical radius, may signal a new type of death by "spaghettification." We calculate the Reid-Tinianu and Ricci Tidal Displacement Tensors, which reveal a separation of the spacetime into an exterior region, which contains the wormhole, and an interior

In chemically doped graphene, we observe that the Fermi velocity's renormalization significantly impacts the quasiparticle properties, leading to a reduced doping concentration's effect on specific heat and an extended mean-field theory's range of applicability. Moreover, we found that the Luttinger-Ward formalism facilitates a self-consistent calculation of quasiparticle properties and mass renormalization, thus enabling the extension of mean-field theory to a broader range of doping levels.

A newly developed system called MaskedSpeech learns speech representations that combine speech and emotional metadata. This system creates a unique mask sequence for speech segments, linking them to the corresponding emotional metadata through a masking encoder. The interaction between the speech encoder and the metadata encoder is controlled by the masking encoder, which tempers the influence of the speech encoder on the output decoder when a mask is present. The use of the masking encoder allows the traditional speech encoder to focus on unmasked segments, while the decoding stage integrates the masking information into the speech output, resulting in more natural and expressive synthesized speech, particularly when generating speech with specific emotions, as it is achieved through self-supervision without the need for labeled data.

High-dimensional Bayesian Gaussian Process models are increasingly employed in real-world applications, despite their computational intractability in such settings. This research presents a novel approach to posterior variable selection for large-scale Gaussian Process models in a computationally efficient framework. The method involves decomposing the Bayesian Gaussian Process model into its constituent parts and applying a common stochastic factor, whose posterior is efficiently estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo. Subsequently, the No-Effect Level of the selected model is calculated based on its constituent parts and the selected model's posterior. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through an automotive parts sales prediction case study, characterized by its numerous features and observations, and through performance evaluation in large-scale regression and classification problems. The results indicate that the method preserves the uncertainty characteristics of the original model, remains efficient even for thousands of features, and that the selected model generally performs well compared to the full model.

This paper's first section delves into different types of attacks and their variations, providing a detailed explanation of how Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks work, contrasting them with standard adversarial example attacks and discussing their limitations in specific scenarios. We also explore significant differences between MitM and other types of attacks, and present scenarios where MitM attacks are most effective while others fall short. Building upon this foundation, our studies in sections 2 and 3 focus on enhancing the effectiveness of Fermi's and Iggy's adversarial examples against MitM attacks. We are assessing their resistibility against these attacks, alongside that of Bazzi's adversarial examples. To compare their effectiveness, we developed a platform for generating weak and strong adversarial examples. However, our analysis reveals a surprising contradiction: despite their apparent robustness, Fermi's and Iggy's adversarial examples exhibit higher effectivity than Bazzi's adversarial examples. Moreover, our findings indicate that MitM attacks can successfully deceive even DNNs that appear robust against them. Ultimately, the paper discusses implications of these discoveries, along with potential limitations, and suggests directions for further research, as well as strategies for bolstering the resistance of DNNs to adversarial examples.

Social media platforms have become a significant source of climate change misinformation, with false conspiracy theories being the most prevalent form of cloud climate information. To investigate who disseminates this content, a study was conducted to identify the creators of climate change conspiracy theories on Twitter. The results show that conspiracy groups are the primary drivers of this content, with environment-focused communities playing a secondary role. Notably, individuals sharing climate change conspiracy theories are frequently part of established community spaces, utilizing repetition and interactivity to amplify their message within these environments.

The NA48/2 experiment at CERN's NA6S facility conducted a detailed analysis of the rare decay $\eta\rightarrow \eta'\gamma$ in order to investigate $\eta-\eta'$ mixing and search for dark matter. Over ten years of data collection between 1996 and 2006 allowed researchers to accurately locate $\eta$ and $\eta'$ beams and to establish stringent limits on dark matter particle properties. This analysis no longer relies on a Monte Carlo simulation, thus improving the accuracy of the results. All parameter estimates remain within the expectations set by the standard model and yielded disappointing outcomes for finding dark matter. The research also yielded precise measurements of $a_c$ with two distinct methods and determined $\eta-\eta'\gamma$ vertex couplings.

In a general exangulated category $\mathcal{E}$, we determine the precise requirements for Serre duality to hold. Our investigation reveals that $\mathcal{E}$ possesses Serre duality if and only if the maximal exangulated category $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{E})$ associated with it also exhibits this duality. Furthermore, under these circumstances, we find that the further quotient category $\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{E}))$ of $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{E})$ also satisfies this property.

Despite similar post-secondary education systems in the Nordic countries, there are notable differences in field-specific earnings variations between Denmark, Norway, Sweden, and Finland. A key factor contributing to these disparities is the specific post-secondary fields that students choose to pursue. This research investigates the underlying reasons for this difference, focusing on supply-side explanations such as student characteristics and regional features, and demand-side explanations like field-specific earnings and supply elasticity. Our empirical analysis, based on linked individual-major data, reveals that Denmark experiences particularly low elasticity in certain post-secondary fields. Moreover, we find that student characteristics account for a smaller portion of earnings disparities in Norway compared to Denmark. However, a larger portion of the elasticity disparity between Denmark and Norway can be attributed to regional features rather than individual choices. Ultimately, we conclude that supply-side factors play a significant role in the higher elasticity of post-secondary fields in Norway.

We present the concept and current status of a super $J/\psi$ factory as an $e^+e^-$ collider operating at 3.77, 4.01, and 4.16 GeV, and operating at half the intensity of BEPCII but with advanced technology for precision measurements. Its unique position in the energy spectrum enables cutting-edge research in decay and anomaly searches across the 1 GeV to 4.2 GeV range, and provides an ideal environment for investigating the 'grey area' between heavy-flavor and low-mass hadron-resonance physics.

We simulate the accretion of a triple star system via a flow of dark gas 
with a finite pressure and a sound speed of 10% of its accretion velocity. 
Our numerical models reveal that a triple star system only forms when the 
initial angular momentum of a binary is low. 
A hierarchical triple system forms when a binary sits at the bottom of a 
accretion disk or within a dense disk. 
Accumulated gas on a curve around a binary causes an excessive drag force and 
prevents it from gathering mass and grow. 
As a result, a binary in a triple star system shows significantly less growth 
compared to single stars of equivalent mass. 
To form a hierarchical triple star system, an initially low binary 
momentum is needed, which seems to be around the orbital radius being about 
two accretion lengths or about 0.05 times the mass of a solar mass. 
This finding contradicts earlier predictions that hierarchical triple star 
systems would be rare due to a low binary momentum.
This study also shows that a triple star system shows much less growth than 
a single star of equivalent mass, which can be used to detect and identify 
these rare objects.

This study investigates how the distribution of matter affects the universe's inhomogeneous structure and its evolution over time. Focusing on an universe model that accounts for the distribution of matter and energy, it emphasizes the importance of inhomogeneity and its effect on radiation and dark energy components, which are also spatially distributed. Utilizing a perturbation model, the work derives a time-varying equation and analyzes the phase of large scale geometry, which is often misinterpreted as cosmic acceleration. The analysis indicates that considering the universe's global structure is essential for unraveling the nature of dark energy, rather than the universe's phase of cosmic acceleration.

We present a novel method for image segmentation, specifically for images that have been distorted by noise or other interference, by modifying the traditional Mumford-Shah model on a piecewise constant basis. Our model incorporates a soft prior that allows for a greater number of image regions and introduces the concept of soft image partitions. Additionally, we develop a network of soft prior, permitting the model to capture both local and global image characteristics, and derive an efficient optimization algorithm as a result. Our results demonstrate that the model produces superior segmentation in both low-complex and high-complex images, ultimately outperforming existing methods for image segmentation and image restoration.

Researchers have discovered an anomaly in the Fermi-Dirac distribution of a simulated particle species in Dark Matter (DM) simulations, which was found to significant deviations from expected axion-like behavior. A new analysis led to an updated constraint on the properties of ultra-light particles, which may constitute a fraction of Galactic DM. The analysis revealed that a non-Chi-squared based likelihood function is essential to accurately model long-wavelength, large-scale DM structures. Furthermore, the study introduced an enhanced simulation, which revealed a reduced deviation in a different particle mass range compared to an earlier simulation. By analyzing a solar system's gravitational micro-lensing events, researchers obtained new constraints on the possibility of such particles being the sole constituent of Galactic DM.

A cutting-edge technology known as neuromorphic computing aims to replicate the intricate learning processes of the human brain by leveraging analog volatile memory arrays and analog computational circuits, which are analogous to neurons and synapses. By incorporating on-chip learning mechanisms, this approach seeks to optimize computational efficiency through real-time weight adjustments during both computation and learning processes. While the traditional two-phase training method (offline and online) is applicable in the chip's context, there are specific limitations resulting from analog architecture characteristics. To illustrate, a case study of a volatile memristor-based crossbar array shows that a discrepancy exists between the lab and chip results in mean squared error, relative computational error, and the number of iterations for the mean-boltzmann machine, which are all key evaluation metrics. Notably, this discrepancy is exacerbated in the case of online learning compared to the traditional batch mode, taking specific system parameters into account. Overall, there is a pressing need for adjustments to the conventional, typically on-the-chip applied methods of modeling, training, and evaluating neural machines with analog memory components to ensure that they are suitable for analog systems.

We have developed a theory to understand coronal "noise storms," referencing a work by Ofman et al. (2006). By analyzing data from multiple satellites, including UVI on SOHO, UVCS on SOHO, and SDO/AIA, we have modeled these storms mathematically and observed their behavior. These noise storms exhibit characteristics similar to wave propagation, increasing in intensity, strength, and size over time. This phenomenon can be explained by two possible mechanisms: the storms act as self-sustaining waves or as self-sustaining jets. These noise storms have unique properties: their intensity, strength, and growth in size all follow specific power laws. These power laws can be used to distinguish between the two mechanisms. Additionally, we have observed that the spatial distribution of these noise storms follows a specific pattern, whether the mechanism is self-sustaining wave or self-sustaining jet. This research has significant implications for our understanding of solar physics.

We have developed an innovative miniaturized magnetic-optical trap (MOT) integration. By combining an acousto-optic deflector and magnetic coil array within a single package's planar interface, our novel design achieves enhanced MOT loading rates. Additionally, the reduced size of this hybrid MOT simplifies its vacuum system and lowers its overall size. We have successfully demonstrated a miniaturized Rb MOT using this innovative integration, and observed a $6 \times 10^7$ atom population loading efficiency, which exceeds the typical atom count in玻尔兹曼 equilibrium by an order of magnitude.

The relatively dim luminosity of supermassive black holes such as Sgr A* and M87* is thought to result from a regulation mechanism that controls their radiative output. In this study, we investigate the potential impact of an accreted boundary layer on this self-regulatory process. If the boundary layer reflects a substantial portion of incident radiation, it could provide a source of energy that helps to maintain a balance and keeps these black holes at their observed luminosity levels. Utilizing a multi-layer accretion model, we calculated the boundary layer properties and its radiative output for Sgr A*, M87*, and an array of intermediate-mass black hole candidates, and then compared these results to the observed luminosity spectra of X-rays. Our analysis suggests that a boundary layer with a thickness to radius ratio of 0.1 to 0.3 and a temperature of 10^7 K to 10^8 K is needed to produce the observed luminosity and spectral energy distribution from these hot gases. Moreover, this model is consistent with previous theories about the role of boundary layers in black hole physics, such as the generation of black hole induced magnetic pulsars and the accretion processes that feed the intermediate black holes which then seed massive black holes.

We investigate the impact of an accelerating neutral atom on a nearby reflective surface, a more intricate extension of the Unruh effect. The presence of the mirror amplifies the complexity, making it an ideal real-world scenario to examine. We utilize a non-relativistic quantum framework to model this situation, accounting for the atom's motion and internal state transitions. The presence of the image dipole associated with the atom around the mirror leads to altered spontaneous emission patterns and the Purcell effect. The image dipole's influence is especially pronounced when the atom is close to the mirror and its orientation is parallel to the surface, a scenario not typically observed in existing research.

Our research focuses on the young and dense cluster Westerlund 2, specifically the high-mass stars associated with it. These stars either formed within the cluster or were potentially attracted by its gravitational force. To assess their origin, we examined their kinetic energy relative to the cluster and conducted numerical calculations to determine their bound or unbound status. We found that the high-mass stars with a mass greater than eight solar masses were estimated to have been ejected from the cluster with an efficiency of around thirty percent, similar to other young clusters. A simplified analytical model was found to accurately explain the high-ejection efficiency and its correlation with the cluster's speed. This supported the idea that high-mass stars in Westerlund 2 were expelled through binary formation and interactions, as suggested by the Fall-Richardson model. Moreover, we observed the high consistency between the high-mass stars' ejection patterns and those of other massive stars in the Milky Way.

The set of solutions to a special unbounded unbounded variational problem is shown to be non-empty by applying the minimax principle. Furthermore, the associated minimax equation is demonstrated to have at least one non-trivial solution. This principle is illustrated by a specific unbounded unbounded functional used in the analysis.

This research paper explores the potential of integrating handwritten text recognition systems with generative adversarial networks, specifically for enhancing quality of low-quality document images. It proposes an architecture that incorporates a handwritten text recognizer and a generative adversarial network that restores perceived image data, forming a closed loop. When the hand-written text recognizer is fed the generated image, its performance should be similar to when it is fed the original image data. Our written off the line data set is specifically designed for this research and is used to compare the effectiveness of different models, including those using written and offline data sets.

The Text Extraction from ID Cards (TehID) task, a key application in NLP, aims to automatically parse information from various ID card templates. Recent studies have shown that combining MLP classifiers with geometric patterns or using pre-trained NLP models can effectively extract information. This research introduces an innovative TehID approach that leverages pre-trained NLP models to predict the MLP classifier's input by integrating the features of the pre-trained model. Additionally, the proposed method pre-processes the input image to simplify the ID card structure, significantly reducing the number of training samples required and improving accuracy. Experimental results on the TehID benchmark indicate that the NLP-based approach achieves a test accuracy of 87.5%, surpassing the best existing methods. Moreover, the proposed approach demonstrates robust generalization on a limited dataset and excels in end-to-end ID card information extraction.

A key challenge in single carrier transmission in the sub 6 GHz frequency range is channel estimation, which suffers from high pilot overhead, especially when using a short cyclic prefix. This limitation becomes even more pronounced in high mobility scenarios where channel coherence blocks are very short. This challenge is further exacerbated in the design of 6G systems with ultra wide bandwidths. This work aims to address this issue by developing an updated LSTM-based receiver that can adapt to changing channel conditions in real-time with low complexity, using iterative estimation and a combined approach of pilot and data-assisted channel estimation. Compared to traditional methods, the proposed receiver exhibits a significant reduction in error rate (100-1000 fold) while maintaining near optimal performance and spectral efficiency. Additionally, simulation results show that the receiver can support high data rates of up to 10 Gbps using QAM modulation, even when the transmission duration is as short as 1 ms. This low complexity design and superior performance make the proposed receiver a viable solution for future 6G systems with high mobility.

We present a novel deep learning-based approach to improve image quality in low-resolution astronomical images, utilizing an image super-resolution network. The algorithm is based on convolutional neural networks, incorporating an unsupervised masking self-supervised learning technique to generate high-resolution training data from existing low-resolution images. A newly developed loss function, which combines both pixel-wise and frequency domain metrics, is crucial for the effectiveness of the model. The super-resolution network consists of a series of convolutional layers, an accompanying skip connection system, and an output activation function. The enhanced method is demonstrated to outperform existing algorithms in terms of both visual image quality and overall accuracy.

A new optimization algorithm is presented, leveraging artificial neural networks to determine the optimal parameters for black box simulators engaged in multiobjective global minimization tasks. Notably, the approach sidesteps overfitting by refraining from utilizing derivative information in the learning process. To account for the non-stationary nature of the "learning task," the algorithm employs an adapted Minkowski distance to construct a methodical learning scheme. Furthermore, a binary representation is employed for the neural network and an optimized learning rate management is integrated, both derived in appendices for contextual integration. The algorithm is thoroughly tested on two-dimensional, multi-objective problems, with associated code made available online at the provided URL address.

In April 2021, the ECFA Early Career Researcher (ECR) panel was established and held its first meeting in October 2021. This panel was set up to support ECRs within the ECFA system, particularly in areas of communication, general management, and strategic planning. During a hybrid eConference on 17 and 18 May 2022, ECRs shared their insights on current challenges and the opportunities they face in AC-TC operations.

This research demonstrates a method to map graphene's unique properties onto line waves in the optical range by employing a patch of graphene inscribed with an intricate nanoscale pattern. Its graphitic component interacts with substrates featuring fine nanostructures to support these specific wave modes, which are significantly enhanced by the patch's unique electronic properties. The approach has been empirically verified and shows great promise for developing next-generation photonic devices, particularly in simplifying the microelectronics needed for graphene's functionality and expanding the possibilities for integrating it with other materials.

This research investigates multi-human multi-robot interactions within the Federated Learning framework. The key characteristics of Federated Learning enhance the FFA by ensuring that data collected through human-robot interactions remains confidential and secure. The study contributes in three main areas. Firstly, a novel task coordination approach is presented that leverages a central server and multiple human-operated robots to achieve a collective goal, with each robot training its own model using local data and contributing only the updated parameters to the server. Secondly, the paper examines the impact of asynchronous updates on this task-coordination method. Lastly, the study evaluates the effectiveness of the approach in comparison to a traditional centralized system.

A novel method for bias-corrected estimation of distributional properties is proposed, focusing on arbitrary statistics that converge at the standard n^1/2 rate and based on an arbitrary distribution. To address the issue of bias reduction resulting in non-smooth estimates, our estimator applies a smooth adjustment. We evaluate the performance of the proposed method through simulations and apply it to bias-corrected estimation of civil penalty bias and distributional characteristics of civil fines imposed by New York City's Department of Consumer Affairs.

A pivotal task in knowledge graph analysis, link prediction involves estimating which entities are connected in the graph. A typical approach to this problem is trained using a large dataset of entity tuples from the knowledge graph. However, this method relies on implicit entity relations that were not explicitly extracted and thus may be inaccurate due to implicitly derived patterns. In contrast, we take the method of knowledge graph representation learning that is based on the explicit extraction of entity relations as the starting point. A novel algorithm we develop learns a knowledge graph representation by directly using structured entity relations through an attention-based relation embedding model. Experimental results we obtained from the Facebook Knowledge Graph show our proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in link prediction. Notably, we find that adding a small auxiliary dataset to training significantly boosts performance, even when the main training dataset consists of entities with noisy, implicitly derived relations.

In the context of three-flavor nonlinear sigma model, the DEYE mass was previously determined to order $O(e^2)$. This paper re-evaluates the Debye mass in the presence of a baryonic potential, finding that at leading order it is unaffected, but that at next-to-leading order (NLO), it acquires a contribution proportional to the potential itself. The proportionality coefficient is found to be identical in both the SU(2) and SU(3) QCD theories. The paper's findings also serve as a vital input for the matching between the Wilson operator expansion and the three-flavor nonlinear sigma model.

A detailed study of the magnetic structures of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 was conducted using neutron diffraction at various temperatures below the rare earth ion's ordering temperature, and this data is compared with that of CaTbO3 and CaNdO3 intercalinated ferromagnets. Interestingly, while Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 exhibit complex magnetic patterns, both CaTbO3 and CaNdO3 exhibit simple ferromagnetic alignment. Upon examination of the ruthenium ions within Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7, it becomes apparent that these ions establish an ordered arrangement of moments, consisting of two distinct sites labeled Ru1 and Ru2. A comparative analysis of this ordering in Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 shows that both sites exhibit identical orders for these ruthenium ions, with Ru1 and Ru2 ions both exhibiting antiferromagnetic behavior. This phenomenon suggests a similar mechanism governing this ordering process. A Landau theory model supports this interpretation of Ru ions' magnetic ordering within Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7.

This research focuses on the local-functional representation of neural networks, 
employing a functional approach where the local weights are determined by a positional 
encoding function rather than individual entries. The local representation offers enhanced 
generalization capabilities, particularly efficient for signals with lower dimensions. 
We offer an analytical assessment of the positional network's expressive capacity, 
alongwith experimental evidence demonstrating its efficacy in various benchmark tasks 
and enhanced generalization performance for low-dimensional signals. Moreover, this study 
explores position-based residual networks and investigates their effectiveness in various 
benchmark datasets and deep learning competitions. The source code is publicly available 
at the specified GitHub repository.

We introduce a new type of probabilistic model that is semi-generative in nature for analyzing causal data, proposing a structural equation model where the effects and causes of a target variable T are represented as distinct data representations. These encodings satisfy a specific assumption: T can be modeled independently of its causes given its effects. Utilizing a neural module, the model's parameters are optimized through constrained optimization: an "independence" constraint requires the representation of T's causes to be orthogonal to its encodings, while the orthogonal constraint dictates the relationship between the model's input and output spaces. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing methods in various semi-supervised and causal transfer learning scenarios.

Recent research in the analysis of deep learning systems has been exploring its geometric properties to understand how algorithmic design and architectural structure influence learning performance. This paper extends that investigation to statistical inference of deep learning models by analyzing a generalized Bayesian approach to modeling uncertainty in trained models. By applying generalized linear model techniques, we develop a successful inference method for distributed learning and weighted quadratic propagation, revealing that data weighting in weighted inference aligns with arithmetic weighting during training, while decentralized training leads to geometric averaging of weights. Moreover, we characterize the uncertainty of inferred parameters in relation to trained learning coefficients, highlighting the importance of analyzing geometric properties in deep learning not only for optimization but also for statistical inference.

The distribution of lattice minima within a random collection of lattices formed by integer points in a randomly oriented $d$-dimensional box, as described by Beskou et al., is explored. The impact of different field properties on the distribution of these minima is investigated, particularly for cubic fields, and a parametric study showing how the distribution changes with field characteristics is presented. The study reveals that specific choices of irrational numbers in the generating vector can lead to the lattices not having a unique minimum, and that the density of such vectors increases with the trace of the square in a predictable way. Furthermore, numerical investigations suggest that certain values of the trace can lead to the appearance of second-order minimums, and that such instances are relatively rare.

Grasping the underlying mechanisms of deep neural networks is crucial, but their complex nature makes them difficult to interpret, particularly with regard to how they learn features, covariates, and their associated weights. In this context, we introduce a novel, unified theoretical framework for layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) that prioritizes the propagation of relevance in neural networks. By integrating our framework, which is straightforward and easy to apply, we can determine the relevance of inputs that aligns closely with the neural activity of a trained model, without compromising the established correctness constraints. Furthermore, we apply our framework to interpret a notable phenomenon observed in neural networks known as the alignment effect. By extending our LRP framework, we also successfully interpret the emergence of reversible features in neural networks, revealing how these features develop over time during the training process. This analysis explains how reversible features, despite initially appearing to be chaotic, gradually become essential for accurate generalization in trained models.

The R-associated Stirling numbers of the second kind, a generalization of the well-known Stirling numbers, were introduced by Zhang and further explored by multiple researchers including Qi, Wei, and Zhou. These numbers represent the count of partitions of an n-element set into r-associated subsets, where each subset must contain at least r+1 elements. In this paper, we introduce novel differential and integration methods for the r-associated Stirling numbers, along with their corresponding generating functions. Our findings also include the derivation of a new recurrence relation and several identity equations related to these numbers.

We introduce a set of coordinate-free mathematical tools for describing long-range ordered materials with broken inversion symmetry in a layered structure. The derived notation classifies irreducible domains based on the layer indices and inverse maps between inverse layers, which can be represented as a shift in log base $q$. The classification is completed with the introduction of a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ factor based on how a specific atomic position shifts under inversion. There are a total of eight distinct domains for materials with uniform plane spacing. The unified mathematical framework also identifies layer-dependent phenomena and interplay between electronic and structural distortions in materials like $\mathrm{TiI}_3$.

The $S/O(N+1)$-invariant path integral for free scalar field theory is derived when restricted to an $S^{N+1}$ of the same diameter as de-Sitter space $(M_{dS,3})$. This is done using a discrete series of unitary representations of the de-Sitter group. The resulting path integral matches the continuum limit of a lattice, but with a maximum momentum resolution linked to the sphere's diameter and equivalent to the de-Broglie wavelength with a Compton wavelength matching the de-Sitter space diameter. Additionally, this approach is consistent with general relativity, where it represents a lattice, and the time component of a geodesic matches a free field solution with its associated frequency given by Compton's formula.

We're introducing a method for improving the output of neural networks that uses complex values in an affine coupling framework. This approach boosts the sample diversity and distribution accuracy of Monte Carlo simulations. We integrated this enhanced affine coupling layer with other network architectures to develop a translation-invariant model for predicting molecular representations. We examined this translation-invariant model's performance compared to its standard and real-valued counterparts using three models with varying levels of complexity: three, 15, and23 hidden layers. We evaluated the network's sampling efficiency based on how long it took Monte Carlo simulations to reach a steady state and its ability to accurately model molecular distributions. We conducted the simulation studies on three datasets: small, medium, and large collections of protein structures, showing that our approach significantly improves the sampling efficiency and distribution accuracy over its real-valued alternative.

In this study, we explore a U(1)_F flavor symmetry breaking scenario in a composite model. By utilizing the highest chiral representation of the SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y gauge group, we adjust the potential to achieve the most minimal number of fermion doublets while satisfying this symmetry, ultimately forming matter condensation that breaks the symmetry. We propose a mechanism in which the hierarchy of mass between the top and bottom quarks arises from the breaking of the U(1)_F flavor symmetry, driven primarily by the heaviest fermion's Yukawa coupling with the Goldstone boson field. We further examine the stability of the vacuum and find that an extremely small epsilon parameter (0.00184) is required for the model to remain vacuum stable, consistent with the desired mass hierarchy of m_t ≈ m_b. We also analyze the Goldstone boson masses within the model.

Vocal performance prediction machines, known as VPPMs, are AI-driven tools designed to assist singers in refining their vocal performances. Although these programs are helpful in educational settings, they present vulnerabilities to potential abuse if an attacker manipulates their feedback. Our research focuses on this vulnerability by exploring how a malicious actor can exploit VPPMs to create voice aliases that mimic a target's voice and provide superior singing performance. Using a multi-objective genetic algorithm, we successfully generated such voice aliases from a single sample of a target's voice, which were then added to a VPPM database. When compared to the original audio also drawn from the same singular sample, the alias voices were found to produce superior singing performance according to the feedback and performance metrics given by the VPPM. Subsequent experiments tested the robustness of these voice aliases against acoustic modifications and variations in the number of samples used, which were also discovered to increase the malicious voice's similarity to a target's voice. Finally, we assessed the potential impact of noise generated by the voice alias on a target's singing performance and found it resulted in negligible changes.

The performance of big language models is notably affected by the size of their training data. Research into fine-tuning these models has mostly concentrated on enhancing their proficiency in specific tasks. In contrast, there has been very little investigation into how well these models can be adapted to new, unfamiliar languages. Our study reveals that the features contributing to a model's data efficiency in one language are often transferable to another. Therefore, the study focuses on boosting a model's ability to tackle a new, unseen language by selecting distinct training data subsets from its original corpus and examining various features of this selection process. A key discovery shows that training on a diverse range of data types, such as different word lengths and script styles, significantly improves a model's ability to fine-tune in new languages. Moreover, these findings offer practical insights into optimizing the initial pre-training of large language models for enhanced multilingualism and flexibility. In fact, the proposed techniques increase a model's accuracy by 4-14% in a zero-shot setting when evaluated on a new, unfamiliar language.
