This research paper explores the application of k-arXivRanking (k-arK) function for
dimensionality reduction and learning tasks within the arXiv preprint dataset,
an extensive collection of machine learning training data, and investigates whether
this tool surpasses traditional embedding methods in effectiveness. Additionally, it
introduces an extended version of the k-arK function to account for time-dependent
labeling, enabling precise document classification and prediction in various domains,
such as medical diagnosis. Experimental findings indicate that the modified, temporally
sensitive form of the k-arK function achieves superior performance in classification and
prediction tasks while also demonstrating enhanced accuracy in document classification
over the past decade, with an average improvement in scores.

This research explores theoretical implications tied to Computation Tree Logic. It's proven that under specific conditions, a massive increase in memory requirements is necessary for certain logical models to function correctly - specifically models assessing full PTIME programs' computational power (in terms of both runtime and memory usage). Furthermore, should certain complex logical formulas be shown to be decidable at an efficient rate (in FPT complexity), this would mean that the computational models used to assess all possible programs on finite alphabets don't require infinite memory to function, thus implying the equivalence of computational models with and without access to infinite memory, in turn suggesting the equality of two complex computational models. It's also discovered that decisions regarding the validity of certain simple logical formulas (in LCPT) are undecidable. In contrast, if these formulas were found to have efficient decision procedures, this would mean the existence of the most powerful computational model is equivalent to another, more limited model (in terms of runtime and memory requirements), allowing for more constrained data processing.

A finite set of elements defines a ring's identity, and we say two rings are equivalent if they share the same identity. We say a ring I in an equivalent ring R is a $\tau$-ideal if it is minimal and non-zero. In this paper, we investigate the existence and existence uniqueness of certain types of $\tau$-ideals in commutative rings with identity, and local rings, based on the structure of their quotient rings.

Social media platforms are where various groups discuss issues related to their interests and concerns, making it essential to understand the narratives they create. Social listening tools are used by listening agencies to track social media discussions on specified topics, and analyzing its output is a potential way to identify narrative formation. Listening agencies require insight into which social media posts contribute to group discussions and how the content within those posts should be interpreted. This research introduces a listening metric called Listening Narrative Influence (LNI) that assesses the extent to which a posting user contributes to group discussions by listening metric. A weighted average approach is used to incorporate the significance of each mention in a listening metric to the posts' overall influence. Two neural machine reading models are then employed to interpret the narratives within each listening metric. An experiment was conducted on four different topics to test this new metric and gained the validation of domain experts. Furthermore, a simple model called Listening Narrative Attribution (LNA) is proposed to identify the users contributing to group discussions within a specified topic.

This work presents a method for space-time event detection that builds a single detection model for all spatial scales. Unlike existing methods that rely on manually setting a specific spatial resolution for each event, our approach automatically handles events occurring at different spatial scales. After training, our model can analyze videos without predefining a specific spatial resolution for each event. An innovative multi-scale convolutional layer in our Siamese network compares synchronized visual patterns at various spatial resolutions to identify events. We evaluate the performance of our system on seven benchmark datasets by measuring its ability to accurately detect and classify events across different spatial scales.

The distribution of young galaxies is impacted by their star formation processes, which is also related to their halos and the surrounding matter distribution. To gain insight into the evolution of this relationship, we need to consider not only the inherent properties of the matter distribution but also its effect on the CMB. The incorporation of CMB lensing data in galaxy-based cosmological studies can help eliminate galaxy selection bias and improve our understanding of the matter distribution, which also helps limit the influence of galaxy-halo mapping on the final result. The extent to which future lensing observations will constrain galaxy-based cosmology depends on several factors, including the depth and quality of the galaxy sample, its star formation rate, and its spatial distribution. The most relevant region to consider is around the turn-over scale. For a dataset with future CMB stage 4 quality, we can expect to significantly limit a potential bias in future spectroscopic surveys, which can have a significant impact on a study of the matter distribution and $w_0w_a$ cosmology, particularly for a study that is not constrained by CMB data.

The performance of an artificial neural network is significantly impacted by deep learning's inherent weaknesses. A novel approach is proposed to enhance the reliability of neural networks by increasing their resilience to extreme distorties. The method works by learning an adaptive input space reduction system that focuses on the most crucial input dimensions. This system is implemented as a mask learning problem within a neural network framework. By using computational resources efficiently, the model can be trained to optimize its performance. Computer experiments validate the method's ability to make neural networks more resistant to extreme distorties.

The rapid dissemination of false information on social media poses a significant threat, especially by causing panic and disrupting societal order. Understanding how to effectively combat and mitigate the spread of false information is crucial. The present study employs an advanced mathematical model, based on system theory, to analyze the impact of false information on its targets. The analysis involves defining key features and searching for optimal strategies to limit the effectiveness of false information. The outcomes reveal that using advanced data science methods to predict and locate features can significantly increase the impact of false information, with even minor adjustments leading to substantial changes in its effectiveness. Furthermore, it is found that false information's impact diminishes over time at an exponential rate, with its rate of decay tied to its maximum potential impact.

A newly proposed method for evaluating low-dimensional features from hyperspectral images has been developed to classify individual image pixels. This method leverages the relationship between the complexity of the original high-dimensional data and its low-dimensional representation to measure the ability of various dimensionality reduction techniques to reconstruct data significance. Unlike traditional methods that assess classification performance to evaluate low-dimensional features, this method provides a more reliable measure of feature quality that promotes finding optimal high-dimensional low-dimensional maps. Experimental results using realistic hyperspectral data show that certain techniques, such as LPP, SMIPP, and L2ISDA, exhibit superior classification performance and better ability to reconstruct data significance compared to other methods, such as LDA, L1PP, and maximization of Fisher's discriminant ratio.

This research paper explores techniques for deeply compressing Deep Neural Networks. Several approaches, such as Pruning, Quantization and Distillation have been developed to achieve this. A novel framework for end-to-end network compression is proposed, incorporating Pre-trained ConvNet Pruning with Provable Analysis, Adaptive Distillation, and System-Specific Quantization. The Pruning and Distillation steps occur in an iterative manner, while the Provable Pruning ensures deep neural network structure integrity and the Distillation introduces a novel approach of knowledge transfer between a teacher and student network. The Provable Pruning with Adaptive Distillation results in a simplified student network with reduced parameters and operations, followed by a System-Specific Quantization of the student network to achieve the optimal balance between accuracy and efficiency for the target deployment environment. The application of this framework on ResNet-50 for ImageNet classification demonstrates a 75% reduction in FLOPS with no loss in classification accuracy, and when deployed on the NVIDIA T4, it yields a 2.76x speedup and 2.23x memory savings compared to the original ResNet-50, with only 4.04% accuracy loss.

We introduce ProCS, a method for achieving precise protein structures. It uses co-evolution data to determine the positions of atoms within proteins and has been optimized using two techniques. First, Coarse-graining reduces the computational load by representing the protein with fewer, larger particles. Second, multi-stage learning divides the task into simpler stages, starting with rough estimates and gradually refining the results. This approach enables ProCS to accurately fit the protein's backbone and side chains, and has demonstrated its effectiveness through comparison with high-resolution experimental data and previous studies. Notably, ProCS achieves a level of accuracy comparable to the best tools for fitting side chains, and our process is transparent and can be easily accessed at https://procs-benchmark.com/.

This study introduces a novel view on optimizing KL Divergence as a more effective alternative to cross-entropy for certain regularized auto-encoders. It reveals that using the entropy term as part of the KL Divergence performance metric enhances the quality of reconstructed data and improves the accuracy of Aesthetic and Grading analysis results. Moreover, it's observed that average variational inference methods generally achieve better outcomes compared to their deterministic counterparts, with different choices of the $\beta$-parameterization method leading to different outcomes on various models. Consequently, this research suggests that under-represented loss functions like KL Divergence can be outperformed by a combination of cross-entropy and entropy regularization, which addresses the under-researched area of variational loss functions in the area of generative modeling.

The parquet amplitude is a crucial concept in many-body theory, yet it remains an open problem to derive it accurately using the Hamiltonian. First proposed in the 1960s and 1970s by various researchers, several methods were proposed to calculate the parquet amplitude, but they all had significant flaws. A new approach by Chen et al. in 2021 offered substantial improvements, exhibiting both conservation and crossing symmetry. In this study, we compare the behavior of the parquet and Hamiltonian-derived amplitudes in respect to energy and momentum within the physical spectrum, and the results indicate that these amplitudes exhibit similar trends. Additionally, we perform three-dimensional parallax analysis of the parquet and Hamiltonian-derived amplitudes, and the experiments suggest a possible discrepancy in their behaviors. This research opens up new avenues for investigating quantum field theory and high-energy scattering processes.

Experimental studies with linear polarization have shown a polar-dependent absorption spectrum in monolayer TiSe2. This research explores the possibility that an excitonic state is responsible for the observed changes. Through calculations based on density functional perturbation theory, we find that the excitonic resonance in TiS2 has linear polarization characteristics, but its direction is perpendicular to that of the material's layers. Experimental data reveal a shift in absorption intensity at lower energies in a phase that exhibits charge-density waves. This shift is consistent with the size and properties of calculated excitons in TiSe2 and is comparable to values predicted by self-consistent many-body theory. The experimental data also indicate a critical temperature limit, as well as the coexistence of exciton and charge-density wave states in TiS2.

In text-based risk reporting systems, dispatchers receive various categories of event reports from users via different channels (phone text message).  They gather essential information essential for further investigation and response (location type of incident).  While systems often include decision support tools to guide dispatchers in asking relevant questions, there is limited understanding of their typical information needs.  To address this, we analyzed a substantial dataset of 14022 real-world report interactions from 122 dispatchers.  The study revealed patterns in the information that dispatchers ask for across different event categories and found that they frequently deviate from the questions suggested by the decision support system.  The study emphasizes the importance of incorporating real-world expertise into the design of intelligent question-asking systems to improve their effectiveness and usability.

We have calculated the topological coefficient of the Fermi surface along a specific crystallographic plane in Li$_2$FeSe. This coefficient correlates to the difference in magnetic susceptibility between 1D and 2D electron systems within that plane. Observations show that the susceptibility in LiFeAs exhibits 3D-like properties at magnetic fields aligned with the 00l axis, while it mimics 2D behavior in directions like 100 and 0k0. Moreover, when the field is along 110, the susceptibility displays intermediate characteristics between 1D and 2D. These findings indicate that the magnetic properties of LiFeAs are intrinsically three-dimensional, yet the influence of the crystal structure introduces aspects of 2D-like magnetic behavior.

A new, innovative active learning method has been developed that combines minimum uncertainty and maximum diversity principles to efficiently choose training samples while maintaining a minimum information level. By leveraging an innovative semi-supervised minimax entropy approach, the algorithm adapts under a strict constraint and balances various characteristics of partially labeled datasets. The resulting selection strategy minimizes both uncertainty and redundancy in unlabelled samples, and we propose a novel diversity-based metric that uses the Fisher score to assign partial labels based on the similarity of their manifold neighbours, which serves as a soft constraint in sample selection. The proposed method relies solely on a fisher score calculation, which has an extremely low computational complexity of (2+N)/(2+Kd), where N and K are the number of training and partial samples, and d is the dimensionality. Experimental results on seven diverse, real-world data benchmarks have demonstrated the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art active learning algorithms by achieving better accuracy while requiring less data annotation effort.

We've gathered a large, comprehensive music database of 1 million MP3 files, consisting of top 40 popular songs from each decade from the 1950s to 2010s. Using a MusicMP3 feature extractor, we've converted each song into a feature vector and analyzed the resulting dataset. This enabled us to investigate the timbre similarity among the songs and found a distinct cyclic pattern in the similarity. This discovery may provide valuable insight into future music listening habits and has led to the creation of a unique musical art style. The comprehensive database of these songs can be accessed at the provided repository link.

This investigation examines countable infinite stochastic processes with reinforcement on a non-negative number line. A couple of important conditions are imposed upon these processes to ensure that block probabilities remain consistent with certain random measures as time increases without bound. Under such circumstances, we establish several criteria, derived from the properties of time-unnormalized weights sequences, that guarantee the same theorems from almost sure reinforcement processes apply. These criteria can be expressed in terms of inequalities involving time-critical parameters for the given stochastic processes with reinforcement. Consequently, new proof is offered for two fundamental conditions - the strong law of large numbers and condition A - for specific processes with reinforcement. Additionally, we establish new results regarding the asymptotic behavior of block frequencies, their variance, and central limit theorems under certain parameter constraints.

This paper proposes a framework for understanding logic by defining the meaning of principles through the methods of their proof. Research in proof-theoretic semantics is characterized by two key concepts, the first being containment – the idea that the set of valid statements derived from a principle should be limited to those inherent in the language itself. The second concept establishes a relationship between principles, allowing for a analysis of how they relate to one another. The paper explores this notion in the context of higher-order classical reasoning and uses it to establish a correspondence between principles and to demonstrate the equivalence between certain logical principles and to derive new equivalences and a notable result regarding implication exclusion.

The development of a reward function for the preference of large language models has become a crucial area of research, requiring a balance between human interaction and automated processing. However, the current method of comparing outputs one at a time is inherently slow, prompting an exploration of more efficient techniques. An effective solution has been devised that leverages human annotators' ability to handle multiple comparisons at once. By building on past knowledge of reward functions and incorporating feedback from human evaluators, this approach scales up their annotations and combines them with pseudo-comparisons generated through inferences, ultimately facilitating the learning of a reward model. An experimental evaluation of the technique has confirmed its effectiveness, revealing that it can reduce the time required for human annotation by as much as 60% while maintaining the same level of reward model performance.

The Smyth powerspace construction, a fundamental concept in domain theory, is explored. It is shown that this construction does not necessarily maintain core-compactness, although it does maintain it for countably based core-compact domains. Additionally, we demonstrate that core-compactness is kept when applying the Smyth powerspace construction to finitary domains. The proof of this latter result relies on a stronger form of core-compactness, known as strong core-compactness, which we show is present in finitary domains and is equivalent to core-compactness for BC-ret retracts of these domains.

Building on earlier assumptions for the motion of uniaxial Bose-Einstein condensates described in \cite{ESZ20, \cite{ESZ21} and \cite{SOT22}}, we examine the dynamics of two loop configurations each containing two vortices with distinct topological charges. A key advancement involves defining a new configuration space that takes into account the enclosed areas, and through this space, we define a metric that reflects the energy differences between the configurations. Furthermore, we develop an implicit system of ordinary differential equations that describe the time-dependent behavior of this configuration space and demonstrate how the global structure is influenced by its boundary dynamics.

We've modified the popular Augmented inverse regression proportionality weight estimator to make it more robust and less sensitive to extreme values. This version of the estimator includes a penalty to constrain the machine learning component, although it may slightly reduce its efficiency. Research has demonstrated that this particular penalty optimization method surpasses other commonly used methods in terms of stability and efficiency.

This study explores the application of lattice QCD in analyzing real-world and simulated experimental data, with a focus on primarily two-aspect and the reasons behind it. The heavy quark in the study is the tau, whose relatively larger mass makes it more suitable for lattice investigation. The report begins with an overview of the necessary formalism, before delving into the distinct features of lattice simulation and the various observables in the study of real data. The report then examines the calculation of the renormalization constant for the axial vector current, with specific focus on the on-shell method in the study of both real and Monte Carlo data.

In a rotation-assisted annulus made of fluid, initial theories have been developed 
to analyze the behavior of chaotic surface waves that form as a result of convection 
and thermal movement. Through experiments that measure thermal patterns, it has been 
found that these waves in three-dimensional space break down into two distinct types: 
a gully and a ridge. These two types of formations exhibit an interplay where they 
surround each other in a balance of forces, much like weather systems on Earth. To 
understand how these structures behave over time, a simplified model has been 
developed that combines both types of dynamics, resulting in the discovery of a self-

Developing a precise and quick tool to find the best fit for continuous continuous distribution parameters is crucial for computing Bayesian estimators of the quantile return period. We have created a novel Bayesian estimator based on continuous continuous distribution and modelled the logarithm of their negative inverses for the continuous continuous Power Law distribution. We used the Legendre Polynomials and Monte Carlo and Newton algorithms to develop rapid estimators that do not require simulation. We also studied the impact of the hyperparameter m on estimation speed and introduced the Cross-Validation model selection method. We compared our novel estimators with existing estimators based on Monte Carlo, maximum likelihood, and minimum information criteria. We used real data to calculate the best fit for the continuous continuous Power Law distribution. The results show that our novel estimators are accurate and quick.

The approximate controllability of the impulsive heat equation, subject to one control input and finite number of impulses, is studied through the solution of an inverse Hilbert space problem with an ill-posed operator. This is achieved by forming and analyzing the inhomogeneous forward problem with an associated inverse problem. We establish a theorem linking the approximate controllability to the solvability of the inverse problem in a small neighborhood of zero within the $L^2$ norm. The theorem is then applied to prove approximate controllability under a solvability condition for specific cases with one control input and a single impulse at the final time.

Current methods for out-of-distribution detection demonstrate significant
shortcomings on a range of common and new challenge data, including synthetic images and corrupted data.
Existing methods are ineffective in generalizing to this type of data and are easily misled by it, often providing false positives and poor score calibration.
In our study, we examine the causes of these false positives and identify the weaknesses of different OOD detection methods.
Using a combination of common and new types of challenge data, we show the need for more robust models that can effectively detect out-of-distribution data.
Ultimately, we suggest enhancing model capacity as a potential strategy for improving robust OOD detection.

This paper proposes original methods for generating forces that impact the behavior of molecules, emphasizing the original contribution lies in the discovery that electron currents can exert stresses on the molecular structure, not just the typically studied impact of electric and magnetic fields. The research focuses on the dynamics of molecular motors, initially demonstrating how currents induce internal forces and then the external motion of a GLYCO model system. Furthermore, the study identifies the impact of constraints on the system's dynamics, discusses the influence of electrical parameters and assumes the absence of electricity influences in the systems where the atoms remain within their equilibrium positions.

Our key finding is that if a two-way transducer at a limited number of states produces outputs that are no longer than inputs in any sequence and can be described using a simple state machine with a limited number of states, then its program can be changed into one that only reads input in one direction and acts the same, but instead of ending equivalence, it can end at the same place as the other input, which can also be described using a limited state machine. This new one-way transducer may have an exponentially longer description compared to the original two-way one, based on research on other similar problems. This new one-way transducer may have an exponentially longer description compared to the original two-way one, based on other similar decisions problems. This new one-way transducer can accept the same input, but under a different state of acceptance - instead of accepting any sequence of pairs of inputs where both components are equal, it accepts sequences of pairs of inputs where both components are equal and also equal in any sequence of pairs of outputs - this describes origin equivalence. This new one-way transducer can accept the same input, but under a different state of acceptance - instead of accepting any sequence of pairs of inputs where both components are equal,

Our new method significantly speeds up the computation of $f$-Convolution entry, particularly when utilizing multi-processors. It is up to $128$ times faster than previously proposed algorithms. We redefine key properties and rework the $f$-Convolution, resulting in a novel, computationally more effective operation. This new method leverages symmetry and a divide-and-conquer strategy, enabling efficient parallel execution on various types of processors, including vector and distributed memory systems. Our approach combines matrix multiplication with a new operation called anti-reversal. We provide detailed analysis on time and work complexity for different types of processors, demonstrating that the $f$-Convolution entry can be computed in $\mathcal{O}\left(n^2/\log_{b}n\right)$ operations on an EREW PRAM with $n$-word memory words, a significant improvement of at least two orders of magnitude in efficiency.

GJ 229B boasts one of the coolest, reddest, atmospheric conditions, and as an intermediate object between planets and stars, its study offers significant insights into the process of stellar formation and accretion. This analysis, based on the most sensitive space-based observation to date, the GJ-229B space observation of the infrared, provides crucial corrections to previous models of atmospheric structure. These discrepancies could lead to an incorrect estimation of the object's age, convection depth, mass, and the radius of the area where it was formed. Furthermore, this research includes a detailed temperature profile, a primary mass estimation, and a discussion on the potential source of carbon monoxide absorption in the atmosphere. When compared with other objects of similar conditions, GJ 229B appears unique, likely due to its significantly larger size and mass affecting its thermal balance.

Using spectral density analysis, we studied the presence of tetraquark states in a theoretical framework, focusing on the role of diquark and tetrquark terms, we also considered whether this method could reveal exotic states like the $X(3872)$. The results indicate that the spectral density can be accurately calculated using a simplified method, and that tetraquark states are highly sensitive to diquark correlations and correlations between diquarks and antidiquarks. Furthermore, we found that including a non-zero tetrquark term has an insignificant effect on spectral density.

If search efforts for phenomena beyond the Standard Model are to be effective, it is crucial to have a high level of accuracy in predicting the CW phase within the Standard Model, especially when experimental limits from the LHC and other platforms are close to ruling out all predictions within its model framework. This work aims to develop a systematic method by which the CW phase can be predicted with greater accuracy, taking into account multiple electroweak precision data points as well as a top quark's mass. A detailed analysis in A, S, T space is undertaken, where CW is treated as a free parameter, to determine the allowed regions for new physics models, and ultimately the allowed regions for new physics models, and ultimately the allowed regions for new physics models.

Determining the concentration of infectious aerosols surrounding an infected person remains intricate, with four distinct categories of models - first-principles, agent-based, zone models, and well-mixed - offering varying levels of complexity. While all can be applicable in specific scenarios, understanding their impact on predicting infectious aerosol concentrations has become a focal point. A fundamental approach was undertaken to evaluate these impacts, resulting in a significant discovery - for a typical infectious aerosol, the well-mixed model consistently overestimates concentration by a factor of 1.5. A numerical tool was created to predict this discrepancy with high accuracy (within 0.01% error), and interestingly, the error can actually decrease when multiple infected individuals are present. A web-based predictor is now accessible to facilitate infectious aerosol concentration estimations.

Experimental data for a specific multi-beta decay in $^{136}$Xe were computed using the macroscopic-microscopic model, which involves analyzing decay in $^{136}$Xe and $^{136}$Ba and comparing them to a previously measured relative end-point in support of a recent published value. Notably, this support was based on a specific nuclear transition in $^{136}$Xe and a spin-forbidden transition in $^{136}$Ba. The study also revealed that the previously published value accurately reflects the ratio of two-square root matrix elements for the two considered nuclei. The investigation further showed that both matrix elements in $^{136}$Xe and $^{136}$Ba are primarily determined by specific 2-particle-2-hole states but that additional configuration mixing may occur near the 2p2h energy minimum in the region of these states, which was found to be X50% in $^{136}$Xe and 20% in $^{136}$Ba. The research further showed that both matrix elements in $^{136}$Xe and $^{135,136}$I are dominantly determined by specific 2-particle-2-hole states but that additional configuration mixing may occur near the 2p2h energy minimum in the region of these states, which was found to be 10\% in $^{136}$Xe and

This study proposes two data-driven methods for independently discovering exchanges program violations based on the findings in arXiv:2102.03188. Our approaches utilize uniqueness results to identify discrepancies in a systematic manner, providing two distinct algorithms for analyzing monetary transactions. To supplement this, we present a framework for modeling relationships between entities, enabling the systematic detection of permutations that break uniqueness conditions across various data domains, including ticketing systems, hotel reservations, and financial transactions. Ultimately, these tools facilitate a comprehensive and automated violation detection process, allowing us to uncover anomalies at an unprecedented scale.

Utilizing a constituent quark model, the $F$-wave bottom mesons are systematically analyzed and their masses are computed. The model also shows these masses fit Regge trajectories, with quark model parameters consistent with experimental data. Additionally, predicted decay widths for $F$-wave bottom mesons are wider, with all excited states above ground state mesons potentially accessible at the BESSY-II synchrotron through synchrotron-trapped $\beta$ decays.

In our previous research, we identified an essential characteristic of valid decompositions into patterned pieces. This finding enabled us to take a closer look at theconsequencesforminimalperiodicdecompositions.We found that the validity of Szabados's conjecture depends on the complexity of the pattern in question. This research delves into this relationship, particularly in the context of patterns formed by two dimensions of integers, where we have established that all sufficiently complex patterns validate theconjecture. Furthermore, whereas we previously only verified the lower bound of this complexity, we now verify both the lower and upper bounds, showing that the pattern's complexity is capped at five times minus four. This research also validates the conjecture for the minimum number of times an area must be repeated in a pattern, where we found that five repetitions are sufficient and necessary for certain cases.

We've developed a versatile method to track the progression of coherent structures over time in complex systems. This approach refines the principle of dynamic mode decomposition to create a dynamic mode decomposition with a time-dependent axis, which allows for continuous observation of structured patterns in that axis. The technique is primarily applicable to datasets that don't include time-based information. To illustrate, the method is used to analyze data from Taylor-Green flow simulations and a human lower airway structure. A Python implementation of this method is available online.

This paper utilizes fitness and complexity measures from previous research to evaluate chess openings and gauge player expertise. We develop an approach linking fitness, complexity, and the diversity of game outcomes. By applying this method to openings, we identify underutilized but promising openings with excessive game diversity. Moreover, we apply complexity measures to assign values to individual games, enabling comparisons between players based on game trajectories. This analysis yields both a global and local perspective on complexity, and we verify its consistency across positions. Furthermore, we explore how player expertise affects complexity in chess.

The standard astrophysical process for forming a neutron star via core collapse in a massive star is well-documented, but an additional mechanism can also contribute to neutron star formation through the accretion induced collapse of a white dwarf. This phenomenon can occur in an accreting binary system once a certain limit in mass is reached by a white dwarf, particularly in binary systems embedded in a dense circumstellar disk. We investigate Accretion Induced Collapse in this particular context, where a neutron star forms through the collapse of a white dwarf, surrounded by a dense circumstellar disk, using an integrated code that includes general relativistic hydrodynamics and radiative transfer. This allows us to simulate key new features that arise, such as a massive black hole feeding on surrounding disk material through a shock wave, which is distinct from core collapse due to its early timing and stronger intensity. We explore a range of disk parameters to assess how environmental factors, including density and radiation pressure, affect the formation of a black or neutron star following Accretion Induced Collapse, which ultimately determines the final remnant's fate and may produce observable signatures in binary systems.

We expand on the method developed by Patera and Winternitz to determine the first integrals of Euler-Lagrange equations for higher-order ODEs. Using this integration of the Method of Direct Lie Point Symmetries, we derive the first integrals for specific systems, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator and its extensions, which even include the effect of friction.

Recent advancements in off-white and multi-view shape reconstruction using white images have been found useful, but their potential for sketch-based 3D shape reconstruction is limited due to the vague nature of sketches. A new method called SSP is introduced, which utilizes an expert system to transform sketch projections into white off-white slices and leverages a learned noise removal model to clean up the complex off-white structures. The resulting precise slices are combined to generate a complete shape model. We were able to test our new approach on publicly available datasets for sketch-based 3D shape reconstruction and compared it with state-of-the-art methods. Our results indicate that SSP achieves superior performance due to its use of expert system-guided high-fidelity off-white point cloud synthesis and multiple learning components.

This study presents all-sky maps of the highly eccentric planet HD80606b in
its host star's reflection and thermal radiation. Utilizing known orbital
parameters and a previously established equilibrium temperature distribution, we
found that the reflection component can reach up to 15% of its orbital peak due
to the planet's seasonal variations with its orbital phase. Furthermore, we
examined how adopting a sloped isotherme configuration instead of an isotropic
scatter model affects these calculations. Furthermore, we analyzed how changes
in wind speed impact the planet's thermal radiation distribution, revealing that
faster wind speeds result in higher peak orbital flux. This study represents the
first instance in which reflection and thermal radiation components are mapped
in their entirety around an object's orbital path.

We investigate the formation of cosmic censorship in collapsing fluids with small perturbations to their initial state. We examine a framework in which the total energy and angular momentum remain constant and the only variable components are the mass and angular momentum profiles. With these small variations in place, we demonstrate that the resultant spacetime maintains a smooth and predictable structure similar to its perturbed foreground. We analyze and compare two distinct cases of collapsing fluid: a non-viscous fluid and a fluid with viscosity. Our study reveals that for a mass profile following a specific power law with an inflection point, small perturbations can expose a fluid singularity. This outcome holds true for a range of inflection points in both non-viscous and fluid with viscosity scenarios. However, we discover that in a fluid with viscosity, the speed at which the fluid co-rotates slows near the singularity. This减速旋转effect gives the co-rotating fluid an extended infall time and we find that as the angular momentum and mass parameters decrease, this difference grows and the resulting spacetime becomes increasingly intricate and dynamic.

We employ a top-down approach to establish a rigorous framework for the weak gravity conjecture in the context of the heterotic $U(1)^{12} T_2 \times T_6 / Z_2$ orbifold. By applying the constraints of extremality and incorporating corrections for quantum and thermal effects, we examine two specific $U(1)$ gauge theories with $N_{\chi}$ charged $\chi$-fields and an array of additional charged moduli fields. Our analysis reveals that, in the presence of an extremal black hole, the mass of the black hole must diminish when an additional $\chi$-field is introduced, given that the mass of this new field is not greater than $\sqrt{2}q$ times the appropriate charge for any value of $\chi$. We define a parameter $\alpha$, representing the ratio of the $\chi$-field's mass to its charge, such that $\alpha \leq \sqrt{2}$ is the required condition to satisfy the weak gravity conjecture. Our study also establishes a link between $\alpha$ and $\mathcal V$, a volume parameter, and shows that, while strong coupling is not inherently incompatible with the weak gravity conjecture, the weak gravity scenario is incompatible with a large moduli field volume. We define a parameter $\mathcal N$, denoting the number of light $\chi$-field degrees of freedom, and show that, for a valid weak gravity scenario, $\mathcal

In a sparsely rewarded environment, we address the issue of efficient reinforcement learning by integrating intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. We employ a causal representation learning approach to distinguish the learner's actions from those of the environment and their resulting impacts. Our expectation maximization framework integrates both external and internal incentives to accelerate the causal discovery process. We demonstrate that in a causal graphical model, the learner's actions and the environment's rewards are interdependent, leading to efficient resource allocation when the learner's actions are not directly linked to the rewards. Introducing a intrinsic motivation parameter enhances training efficiency by approximately two-fold in a multi-room causal environment using a simple feedforward transformer. Introducing a causal attention mechanism that prioritizes learner-relevant history factors along with an extrinsic motivation is comparable to training an extra two agent layers.

Recently, a coloured variation of the Poincaré gravity was proposed, offering a dynamic model for coupled gravitational and matter fields. This framework enables the development of numerous coloured or "lower" gravity systems, each corresponding to specific degrees of freedom in physical fields, analogous to the number of massless particles a model describes. We establish a theoretical foundation for coloured Poincaré gravity, deriving and discussing several coloured versions of the Einstein-Hilbert action, including the simplest model with two colour degrees of freedom. Additionally, we illustrate how the principle of least action facilitates the description of particle interactions within the framework of coloured Poincaré gravity, providing a theoretical description of a model that accounts for the interaction between a coloured and uncoloured spin-2 field. This model captures the interaction between two degree-of-freedom and three-degree-of-freedom particles, suggesting a potential mechanism for this phenomenon. We also note that there are other models describing similar interactions that require further research.

Algorithms parameterized by treewidth have been extensively explored for directed acyclic graphs, given the challenging nature of this parameter in such contexts. This study delves into how treewidth can be effectively reduced in specific types of directed acyclic graphs, such as those with limited out-degreewidth or last-level width. By applying these concepts, we can derive new parameterized algorithms with improved runtimes for long-standing problems, including finding the longest path and set cover in directed acyclic graphs. These findings also lead to the development of novel parameterized algorithms for other long-standing problems, such as topological sorting and shortest path problems, by using width parameters that are not based on treewidth.

In this research, we introduce MemoNav, a neural network that aids robots in efficiently navigating large, complex environments by breaking them down into simpler, manageable sections. By utilizing a modular approach to mapping, each part of the environment can be independently compressed and stored in memory as a compact, condensed representation. During navigation, these compressed maps are retrieved and combined to create a unified path. Through our experiments, we discovered that MemoNav successfully adapts to changes in data and seamlessly integrates new environments while maintaining its learned maps. Additionally, we found that MemoNav significantly reduces the amount of information required for successful navigation, making it an ideal solution for large, complex environments.

With the widespread adoption of 5G New Radio, there is a growing need for a future data offload, and as a result, researchers are turning to the C-band for potential 6G integration. The unlicensed 6G integration within the C-band could offer an extra layer of flexibility. Utilizing the C-band's characteristics, such as an extensive available bandwidth and the absence of existing users, is a promising approach for deployment. Our objective is to design a scalable network architecture that supports the deployment of Unlicensed 6G Small Cells in the C-band while ensuring seamless integration with existing cellular networks. We define a unified framework for Unlicensed 6G architecture and present a scalable A6G architecture with three deployment options: network backhauled, backhaul-enabled, and integrated. The mathematical models for each configuration ensure that Unlicensed 6G Small Cells operate without causing interference to the licensed network, while maximizing energy efficiency and data throughput. We also develop a distributed power control mechanism for both integrated and backhaul configurations. Through simulations, we compare the performance of our solutions with that of a dedicated frequency system, and find that our distributed power control strategy efficiently supports A6G Small Cells with improved energy efficiency and data throughput.

We analyze the impact of complex network structure on solutions featuring spatial variations in complex Ginzburg-Landau equations with various interaction types. Specifically, we examine the emergence of spatially heterogeneous solutions resulting from distinct coupling mechanisms: long-range mean-field interactions, or short-range diffusive couplings. Both processes can independently trigger the formation of spatially complex patterns from uniform states, but we show that their combined action leads to more intricate and spatially spatially aligned structures, with the network's topology directly affecting the pattern complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both mechanism type can stabilize coherent structures, such as scrolls and waves, in two- and three-dimensional systems, while the network structure can also influence their dynamics, potentially reducing their period.

Analyzing the long-term behavior of out-of-time-order correlators (OTCs) is crucial for understanding operator growth and scarring in many-body quantum systems. However, existing methods for calculating this quantity are limited to simple, one-dimensional systems without periodic scheduling. To address this limitation, we developed a framework based on tensor networks for efficiently computing the OTC in periodically forced systems with symmetries. By leveraging these symmetries, our approach significantly reduces computational complexity and allows for direct application to qubit systems. Additionally, we derived an optimized algorithm for calculating qubit OTCs with a complexity of O(N^2), which outperforms previous methods. Finally, we extend our approach to continuous systems by applying the tensor network framework to the Haagerup correlation function.

Recent findings from the Compact Accelerator for the Mass Spectrometry and Isotope (CAMIS) project have confirmed the presence of non-sequential decay processes associated with the Hoyle state in carbon-12. The analysis of the decay patterns of the Hoyle state into alpha particles, both individually and in pairs, along with the dual decay paths of the Hoyle state into an alpha particle and a nucleus of oxygen-8, is essential to a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon. To further examine the half-life of the Hoyle state, we suggest a methodology that leverages the CAmount, a 4 $\pi$ angular correlation spectrometer, which was previously assembled at the INFN-Lab Las Gallinassas in Italy.

The fracture of brittle materials is not influenced by the absence of a minimum size for stresses and strains. The emergence of scales like the lattice size in numerical simulations does not underpin crack behavior under extreme loading rates, where scale-free collapse occurs, nor when cracks interact with obstacles of varying sizes. Instead, the fractal nature of cracks at small scales is a result of the limitations inherent in continuum theories when applied to materials with inherent complexities.

We're looking at the role of memory within single-user finite-state approximation channels.
The capacity of such a channel is measured by the best memory size of its inherent stochastic state.
We're using a statistical three-slope characterisation.
Based on this, we define a modified 'zero-error' capacity, which is characterised by the largest single memory unit that is both causal and error-free.
We show that the 'zero-error' capacity is equivalent to the best single memory unit in its finite-state approximation.
Also, we establish the connection between the 'zero-error' capacity, the typical length, the delay, and the typical number of repetitions.
We use this connection as an alternative way to define the 'zero-error' capacity, which is also equivalent to a spectral capacity with single memory unit.
Finally, we explore how adding or limiting memory within a single user affects its statistical shape.
We discover that the modified 'zero-error' capacity has an increasing shape with respect to the memory length.
We establish the continuity, differentiability, and convexity of this capacity with respect to the memory length.
We define the memory efficiency as the ratio between the modified 'zero-error' capacity, the memory length, and the initial value.
We show that the memory efficiency has a single peak and is therefore unimodal with respect to the memory length.

In a superconducting system with both spin-orbit and Zeeman interactions, even a moderate external magnetic field can destroy the first order topological phase and convert it to a second order topological phase, regardless of whether it matches or exceeds 2Δ. A one-dimensional edge and a two-dimensional surface become a one-dimensional and three-dimensional bulk, respectively, producing Chern bands. A comparison is made between this model and the combined Smith-Vendramini-Zhang model and Higgs model. Studies of Higgs mode responses on the different surfaces and edges show that they can be used to differentiate between the different topological phases.

A benchmark named SEM-TAB, designed for the automated parsing of structured and semi-structured tables, was utilized in the 2021 Google Challenge for Automated Data Extraction for the FIEB project. To evaluate various table parsing approaches, a benchmark consisting of 715 images was created, featuring diverse publishing sources, visual representations, and complex table layouts with varying degrees of structural information. To challenge models in understanding and comprehending table content, a task was included in the benchmark. During a workshop, 14 submissions from 8 research groups participated in evaluation exercises. Strong submissions exceeded evaluation metrics in 3 out of 4 evaluation areas, with 12 teams, 9 of which received successful submissions in each of the 2 sub-tasks.

This brief review explores the essential role of complex numbers in quantum mechanics, demonstrating that understanding this fundamental mathematical concept is as crucial as grasping the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. We also examine common arguments supporting real-number only formulations of quantum mechanics, analyzing their flaws in the process. Furthermore, we explore formulations of quantum mechanics relying on quaternions and other alternative number systems, as well as approaches that eschew numbers entirely in formulating the theory.

To establish a metric dimension in a graph, every node must be capable of identifying the distance to at least one 'reference' node in the graph. In this paper, we focus on graphs with limited 'accurate' identification capabilities - specifically, we look at sub-metrics of original graphs by imposing a maximum distance limit. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and through simulation on power network graphs, that sharply reducing the metric dimension occurs when the maximum allowed distance in a graph exceeds a critical value.

When the change in hydraulic conductivity is relatively small when varied horizontally, we can simplify the complex steady-state flow equation. By assuming a horizontal variation of hydraulic conductivity while considering both vertical and horizontal variations in hydraulic head, we can derive a simple equation that takes into account the steady-state flow. This simplified equation can be applied to various vertical distributions of hydraulic conductivity and has the capability to generate accurate results, comparable to numerical models, within a 10% error margin. As a result, the simplified equation provides a reliable tool for analyzing variable conductivity systems.

This study's primary goal is to develop theoretical models for SO2 and water vapor removal in an O3-UV reactor. A laboratory-scale O3-UV reactor was assembled and studied using an experimental setup and reactor dimensions. A theoretical model for SO2 removal in a O3-UV reactor was developed and compared with experimental data. The results showed that the developed model effectively predicted SO2 removal. The reactor's design, residence time, and water vapor content significantly influenced SO2 removal efficiency.

As a crucial step in developing high-performance neuromorphic systems, this study examines the impact of virtual platform segmentation on real-time simulation speed. By evaluating various partitioning methods on a large-scale neuromorphic IC design, the research identifies key factors that contribute to real-time simulation efficiency. The findings serve as a foundational step for future work on optimizing virtual platform segmentation for high-performance neuromorphic accelerators.

We propose a machine learning framework called Indecision Trees (IDT) that combines structured graph classification with traditional tree models for enhanced interpretability and speed. IDT pre-computes unique sample paths on a graph, feeding them into a tree model. The 'Indecision' aspect refers to selecting tree models for only intricate graph inputs. This approach yields several benefits: it accelerates inference, provides clearer explanations, and achieves better performance, as demonstrated in our experiments with molecular molecular property prediction.

High-dimensional time series data is commonly stored in specialized formats such as columnar files, which can be efficiently analyzed without being converted into a traditional row-oriented structure. Recent advancements in direct format handling have enabled rapid similarity searches for time series data by minimizing pre-processing requirements. Notably, an index method called indTREE has enhanced previous techniques like the NP-index and iIndex-index, which are often paired with extensive datasets. However, the effectiveness of indTREE is limited by its inability to prematurely terminate search processes, a scenario that can be game-changing when working with large datasets. Thus, by integrating early termination, the technique is now better suited for practical applications in specialized data environments. Additionally, the ability to execute horizontal data accesses and execute search processes in the lower level of system architecture significantly improves overall efficiency. As a result, the researchers experienced a hundred-fold performance improvement in certain cases.

Automated code generation within smart code completion systems has significant potential to inspire students and provide valuable feedback; however, the exact impact of our system, named FixMyCode, on student code quality remains unknown. By conducting a controlled study with 100 university students, we measured the system's effect on the assignment completion time, overall code quality, and academic performance. The results indicate that students who utilized FixMyCode wrote code that was 20% more efficient in coverage, though no differences were observed in the quality of implemented functionality, the number of system interactions, or the system's ability to provide detailed feedback, all of which underscores the system's ability to promote code quality without excessive system dependency.

The effectiveness of symbolic surrogate models in clarifying the decisions of black-box classifiers has been established in prior studies. These models can also be utilized to investigate the effects of variations in the input, which is particularly valuable in cases where the black-box classifier operates in a high-dimensional environment with limited understanding of the features it considers most important. We propose the use of single-tree surrogate models to discover the impact of potential features on the decisions of high-dimensional classifiers. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated through experiments with synthetic and real data, comparing it to other interpretation methods and showing its ability to provide a comprehensive understanding of the features that the implicit decision rule relies on.

Over-smoothing and over-regularization present significant challenges in complex network prediction tasks using Graph Convolutional Networks. By examining the theoretical underpinnings of Graph Convolutional Networks, we can better understand the root causes of these issues, which can then inform the design of algorithms to prevent them. This paper also introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework for over-smoothing and over-regularization, consisting of three categories with nine sub-tests. The framework is used to conduct a thorough evaluation of 11 algorithms, leading to a call for a reproducible evaluation methodology in related research.

New dark matter particle production is examined through simplified models that involve either a spin-0 or a spin-1/1 in addition to the dark matter particles, which are assumed to be fermions or bosons. The development of exclusion limits for this scenario takes into account various theoretical configurations and the method of data analysis can be adapted to different cross-section calculations, including those that consider all possible process contributions and the detection of multiple jets. The results also explore how the exclusion limits are affected by including an additional mediator and by considering final states with more than one jet.

We introduce two novel mathematical functions that are deeply connected to the transverse movement of subatomic particles within moving hadrons. These functions are linked to the functions of the Wigner distribution, which is an intrinsic property of the system, and they can be calculated through a process similar to a Fourier transformation. The first function, which we have designated as $T$, relates to the overall movement of the particle, while the second function, $S$, relates to its rotational aspect. The functions, $T$ and $S$, provide a more detailed understanding of the particle's movement, which is now understood to be described by the representation $D^{(1)}$ of the Lorentz group. The relationship between $T$, $S$, and the Wigner distribution can be written as $(T + S) = W$.

This research examines Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Properties in various spaces formed by combining products of the Closed Long Ray and the Long Line with suspensions of ordered sets. We demonstrate that certain categories of spaces, including those in the Grigorieff type, feature the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property when combined with these components. Conversely, we show that an infinite product of these spaces does not exhibit this property, as well as provide evidence that a particular category, involving countable infinite products of Grigorieff type spaces, also lacks this property.

The molecular beam epitaxy of AlGaN systems on SiC is a highly advanced process, but the initial step of graphene formation via chemical vapor deposition varies greatly between facilities, leading to an area of study with significant investigation required to fully comprehend its implications. By utilizing x-ray diffraction, we investigated the molecular beam epitaxy of 30 nm of AlN through SiC-Si graphene interfaces prepared in three different x-ray laboratories with varying degrees of material growth, aiming to determine whether the material quality varies due to differences in initial graphene preparation methods. We observed the growth of a second material phase through silicon, alongside the material that grows through silicon carbide, indicating that differences in graphene preparation methods do not affect the material quality substantially in the current experiment setup. Subsequent studies through x-ray analysis and x-ray reflectometry confirmed the growth of various epitaxial domains through silicon carbide and revealed potential variations in thickness and roughness of the material layers, although the differences were not statistically significant across the three laboratories in the current experiment setup.

Zhang and Lee developed an estimator for $r$, the number of common long-term trends among time series data, which can be affected by extreme outliers. Although the original method provides an almost certain asymptotic result, we show it yields almost sure convergence only for a specific type of distribution and is highly sensitive to data anomalies. We propose an improved estimator with corresponding statistical properties and design an algorithm to determine its value. We assess our method using Monte Carlo simulations and a real data set, demonstrating its improved performance.

Lensing effects within the focal plane of the Abell 222 lens, a galaxy cluster, reveal significant deformations that provide a precise framework for investigating the influence of low-mass entities. Traditionally, gravitational effects of these low-mass entities remain elusive and unaffected by light. Research indicates that the apparent distortions in the lens are substantially impacted by the presence of low-mass entities across a broad mass range, ranging from 10 to 10^6 solar masses. These impacts can be quantified as a percentage decrease in quadrupole and an increase in hexadecapole and octadecapole features, ranging from 10 to 100 times greater, respectively, compared to their original state. Additionally, the effects leave distinct statistical imprints on the distribution of galaxy alignments and elongations within the lens, potentially serving as a detector for low-mass entities across a broad range of scales, potentially down to the sub-parsec level.

One key aspect of technology investment is the interaction between content and internet service providers as they connect through their jointly produced content, resulting in reciprocal investment efforts. Using a noncooperative game model, this study examines how content and internet service providers engage in technology investment in a network of ten interconnected regions. The model uses a Cournot game to determine equilibrium investment levels of co-opetitive parties, and the analysis is supported by simulations. The study's findings reveal how region-specific investment efforts impact content and connection service providers' financial gains, and how these results change when parties move from competitive to cooperative and regional interactions. The research also makes contributions to investment modeling by using a ten-region model which is more representative of the global internet structure than models using a two-region framework.

We've developed a version of "weak naturality" that retains key aspects of naturality, including functoriality and a connection to the functorial behavior of adjunctions. This thought-out exploration aims to stimulate discussion on the topic.

In a recent study, researchers examined the ability of cosmological models to fit current data, and one of their findings involved comparing two types of $ \eta $-attractor models to each other, as well as to a de Sitter model. To the surprise of researchers, both types of $ \eta $-attractor models, which previous studies considered to be part of the same class, actually produce a significantly different set of cosmological data. This discovery highlights the importance of using fit to data as a tool to test and refine inflationary models. Furthermore, this study opens up the question of how the behavior of cosmological models during the non-inflationary period might impact their ability to fit data. To address this, researchers, along with their colleagues, have created new models, including one based on an unusual type of inflation that lasts a short time, which is designed to be compatible with a period of cosmological domination following inflation. To determine if their model is feasible, researchers have carried out a detailed consistency check that includes how to ensure inflation is sufficient enough to produce the right density of cosmological fluctuations and a range of other parameters that are needed, and this, in turn, leads to a question about the behavior of cosmological models during a period called the "graceful exit" out of inflation. This has far-reaching implications for understanding and categorizing the set of quasi-Fuchsian manifolds. We investigated cross-sectional returns distribution to identify structure in financial data. It's interesting to note that moments from a specific asset's returns can be derived from the cross-sectional distribution. Our research focused on whether this structure is random or follows a predictable pattern, and our analysis relied on a large database of US stock returns. Before examining structure, we adjusted for any influence that individual company characteristics had on the cross-sectional distribution. Our main discovery was that moments from the cross-sectional distribution can collectively explain returns variance a week after a specific characteristic-based portfolio is selected. This pattern held for all the characteristics we looked at, and the strength of this pattern varied depending on whether we were considering the first four moments or return variance.

This research introduces a method for identifying cardiac issues in sound environments using limited clean training data. It applies cycle-consistency validation to automatic feature analysis, combining noisy and clean samples while minimizing the use of training data. A carefully constructed analysis network is used for this purpose. The study's results, using a large dataset of ECG sounds and a limited training dataset, show that this method enhances feature consistency, which is crucial for classifying cardiac conditions. It also significantly improves classification accuracy when using classification models with various dropout rates. It is found that this method uses roughly 10% as much training data as previous methods while achieving the same classification accuracy.

The amplitudes for electric dipole transitions from the $2s$ state to $2p$, $3s$, and $3d$ states in hydrogen-like ions have been calculated taking into account contributions from relativistic, electron spin, recoil effects, and corrections due to finite nuclear size. In the process, the leading contributions and their associated correction terms, expressed in powers of $(Z\alpha)^2$, were separated out. Notably, the calculations involved breaking down the transitions into three components labeled Main, Core, and Tail, with the 'Tail' component especially sensitive to relativistic and recoil effects and requiring the use of novel special functions to resolve. In practice, the 'Tail' component was found to be well described by an expansion in $(Z\alpha)^n$, and a library of benchmark values has been developed for the benefit of theoretical and experimental workers on the more complex $2s$-$2p$ transition in muonic hydrogen.

We use equivariant $H^{--}$-cohomology in a combinatorial context to analyze how a finite group acting on a torus 'twists' its structure, with the goal of classifying these 'twists'. We develop an inductive method to determine 'twists' based on the group's derived lengths, with the first step involving classification of actions by affine permutations of order two. We then generalise this to all group actions with a derived length of three, and provide illustrative examples for the group $S_4$.

Establishing a positive departmental environment requires addressing systemic issues
over the long term through setting clear goals, fostering collaboration, and making
intentional system changes. Although individual professors can set a positive example,
lasting change necessitates establishing a vision, communicating with colleagues, and
empowering a group to work towards a shared goal of an improved departmental climate.
This paper outlines the formation of a Student-Affiliated Research Board at UC Berkeley,
which aimed to enhance the Physics, Astronomy, and Astrophysics Department's atmosphere
through events and collaborations. Recognizing the Board's limitations, the students
initiated a comprehensive department-wide assessment to identify specific areas for
improvement and developed a long-term strategy to transform the Physics:AAA Department's
working environment.

This study examines the behavior of the fractional series operator $T_{\mu}$ on $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$ and identifies sufficient conditions for it to be a bounded operator. Specifically, it finds that $T_{\mu}$ does not remain a bounded operator when $\mu$ is outside the interval $[-1+\frac{1}{q}, 1-\frac{1}{p}]$. Furthermore, the research explores a related fractional series operator $M_{\mu}$, which also does not remain a bounded operator on $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$ when $\mu$ is outside the specified interval, even if it satisfies $\mu - \frac{1}{p} \ge -1$ and $\mu - \frac{1}{q} \le 1$.

This research explores the behavioral dynamics of auction participants through simulated experiments based on agent-based models. We examine non-credible second-price auctions with single-bid scenarios, where honest auctions compare against those with buyers or sellers making the sole bid. Our analysis focuses on how sellers exploit a loophole to maximize their benefit without adhering to auction rules. Experimental results show that sellers frequently use this strategy to gain extra profit. However, our analysis indicates that their decisions are not purely self-interested, as they do not always choose the strategy to gain extra profit. These sellers appear to believe they are entitled to extra profit due to their actions, or they think the extra profit is minimal. We also found that allowing sellers to use the strategy as buyers increases revenue, but it also reduces the bid frequency and thus has negative implications for market efficiency.

Evolving anisotropic cosmic structures takes significantly longer than establishing this pattern, prompting researchers to consider whether the universe might exhibit different, smaller-scale anisotropies after a period of time. Although current data lacks precision in measuring anisotropic effects, we investigate how these structures manifest in different epochs. By adopting an approach that approximates the universe as an axisymmetric system, we employ both analytical methods and numerical solutions to the Friedmann equations, which govern cosmic evolution. Our findings demonstrate that the anisotropic rate of change in the early universe mirrors the anisotropic rate of change in the universe a long time ago, but with a crucial difference: in one dimension, anisotropic structures shrink over time due to their inherent properties rather than diminishing due to this pattern, occurring universally across all universes regardless of their isotropic content. However, we discover that universal anisotropic collapse occurs over extremely long periods, approximately six cosmic times since the big bang, suggesting that this phenomenon might be observable in some universes due to differences in long-term isotropy based on their energy and matter content.

In a particular basis for an ordered vector space linked to the Gr\"obner basis of an ideal, we implement a standard basis and apply it to the generators of the Hessenberg variety's local defining ideals, resulting in specific standard monomials. The result is significant as it provides a basic encoding for the coordinate ring of the Hessenberg variety, with an inherent graded structure. The methodology can be generalized for various flag variety subvarieties, offering new polynomial relations for the coordinate rings of these varieties, and potentially enabling parameterization of their coordinate rings through K\"ahler manifolds with compact characteristics.

In the AI art realm, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have made significant contributions, particularly in creating intricate brushstrokes and bringing artworks to life. Nonetheless, current methods for brush generation often fall short in capturing artists' unique styles or adapting to various works. This study presents a new approach, involving the creation of a GAN that efficiently produces brushstrokes on demand, capturing individual styles across multiple artworks. The network consists of two components: a conditional generator that responds to multiple inputs and an encoder that condenses information about brushstrokes, allowing for efficient storage and reproduction of individual styles. Experimental results compare our model with existing models and also with hand-crafted steganographic techniques, demonstrating that entry-level hardware can reproduce complex networks using reduced entry data. Additionally, the study explores the concept of artistic influence and "mixture networks" as a way to explore the boundaries between artistic interpretation and objective analysis.

Recent evidence suggests a flavor anomaly in $K$ and $B$ mesons that may have impacted lepton-flavor universality. This study focuses on connecting this anomaly with light scalar or pseudoscalar extra neutrinos, specifically lepton-flavor specific heavy-neutrinos, which could be generated through a type-I seesaw mechanism. The anarchy assumption is used to analyze heavy-neutrino effects on standard-model-like processes. The search for extra neutrinos is explored via their decay into mesons and lepton's at the Belle II experiment, which could be initiated by flavor anomaly in $K$ and $B$ mesons and enhance the probability of extra neutrinos decaying into lepton's.

We introduce QASPER, a comprehensive Question Answering dataset in the Peruvian Spanish language derived from Peruvian legal documents. This resource consists of 3,541 training examples and 40 testing examples, accompanied by 35 task-specific development sets. To evaluate model performance, we developed five baselines and utilized the QASPER dataset to create a broad question bank. Moreover, we explored model generalization capabilities by creating multiple cross-lingual and cross-domain generalization subsets. To facilitate broad access, we created a user-friendly interface for interacting with the QASPER dataset. Our analysis of the QASPER dataset and associated experiments are available on our website: https://perulegal.ai/QASPER. The QASPER dataset will serve as a pivotal resource for advancing NLP and computational linguistics research within Peruvian Spanish, particularly in the area of legal text comprehension.

Observations of young supernova remnants and the surrounding interstellar medium provide valuable context for understanding supernova explosions. A newly developed radiative hydrodynamic code, called ROSE, is employed to analyze the effects of supernova explosions on the interstellar medium, particularly in relation to young supernova remnant observations. A supernova explosion within a young cluster is simulated, and subsequently, interactions with one, two, or four interstellar medium pockets are both radiative and adiabatically modeled. Our findings suggest that the presence of a supernova shockwave tends to trigger instabilities within the interstellar medium. However, in scenarios where the supernova explosion does not result in a successful expansion, these instabilities are significantly suppressed due to the cooling effect on the shockwave. This implies that observed post-shock regions with smooth surfaces can be used to determine the direction of an implied underlying smooth shockwave. Furthermore, we find that the development of instabilities is particularly favored in cases where an adiabatic shockwave interacts with the interstellar medium, and the radiative loss leads to post-shock shock cooling, resulting in smaller, smoother regions.

This research delves into the analysis and interpretation of Deep Learning models for ADHD detection, using a well-documented pipeline from a previous study. By examining the models, we identified key areas of the brain that are essential for classification and used this insight to create an efficient modification of the models, called Efficiently Trainable Neural Networks (ETNN). In contrast to the original models, ETNN is able to achieve high accuracy (70.46%) while training with a significantly smaller number of brain areas (29 instead of 202). Additionally, we employed Explainable AI (XAI) tools, including Class Activation Indexing and the Shapley Additive Interactions, to visualize the learning patterns of the deep Learning models, thus providing a better understanding of their inner workings and helping to choose the most suitable model for classification. Our findings show that the modified ETNN model can serve as an effective and reliable tool for ADHD detection in clinical settings.

This paper presents an improved version of the interior non-linear Blackwell's theorem by offering an alternative formulation with clearer criteria for ensuring the uniqueness of a non-linear operator's fixed point within the specified interior set. This refinement enhances the original theorem and broadens its applicability. Furthermore, this formulation is pivotal in guaranteeing the uniqueness of a solution to a general non-linear equation in the context of non-linear expectation. By comparing our results with existing theorems on non-linear contracts and non-linear expectations, this work presents novel proofs that resolve long-standing problems with rigorous mathematical foundations.

We demonstrate that for diverse writing domains, computer systems can identify and resolve ambiguous acronyms and referents. Our analysis centers on a real-world dataset from the Legal domain consisting of around 150,000 acronyms and 5,000 legal documents. To learn and utilize context for disambiguating acronyms across multiple documents, we apply a word embedding approach where each acronym instance is represented as a separate word.
